=== spec/scope/application/MainWindow.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from ../rescope import RescopeScope
     3	from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     4	from ../project/open-project import OpenProjectScope
     5	from ../prompt-mode import PromptEditor
     6	from ../prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
     7	from ../editor import EditorScope
     8	from ../palette import PaletteScope
     9	from /ui/components/ribbon import RibbonScope
    10	from /ui/components/file-tree import FileTreeScope
    11	from /ui/components/sidebar import SidebarScope
    12	from /ui/components/diff-view import DiffViewScope
    13	from /ui/components/inset-panel import InsetPanelScope
    14	from ../new-project import NewProjectScope
    15	from ../divergence import DivergenceScope
    16	from ../settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
    17	
    18	export scope MainWindowScope:
    19	    concept: {MainWindowConcept}
    20	
    21	concept MainWindowConcept:
    22	    pitch:
    23	        The main window of the application allowing you interact with all main
    24	        functionality.
    25	
    26	    shape: {MainWindowShape}
    27	
    28	shape MainWindowShape:
    29	    description:
    30	        Maximized window.
    31	
    32	    darkMode:
    33	        The whole window, including popups and notifications, supports a light
    34	        and a dark theme.
    35	
    36	        A "Dark mode" switch in the ribbon's Application tab toggles between the
    37	        two.
    38	
    39	        The choice is persistent: it is saved for the user, across all projects,
    40	        and restored on the next launch. Until a choice has been made, the
    41	        window follows the operating system's light or dark appearance.
    42	
    43	    escape:
    44	        Pressing Esc anywhere in the window, including in an @{EditorScope},
    45	        moves focus to the @{ChatInputScope}. Esc first closes whatever it would
    46	        otherwise dismiss, such as a completion menu or a popup.
    47	
    48	    quitting:
    49	        Quitting while the harness is working on a task or a question, or while
    50	        a build is running, asks first. That goes for Ctrl+Q (Cmd+Q on macOS),
    51	        Quit in the @{PaletteScope}, and the window's close button. The message
    52	        is titled "Quit while a task is running?" and says what is still
    53	        running. "Quit" exits, and "Keep Running" or Esc dismisses it. Asking to
    54	        quit again while it is open doesn't open a second one, and an open
    55	        palette closes first. Prompts waiting in the queue don't count as
    56	        running work, since they are saved with the project.
    57	
    58	    palette:
    59	        Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on macOS) opens the @{PaletteScope} over the window, for
    60	        fuzzy searching the project's files, the application's own commands, and
    61	        the harness's commands, skills, and agents.
    62	
    63	    header:
    64	        ribbon: @{RibbonScope}
    65	
    66	    body:
    67	        sidebar: @{SidebarScope}
    68	
    69	        openFile:
    70	            A file clicked in the @{FileTreeScope} opens in an @{EditorScope},
    71	            in a split beside the chat history: the file on the left taking 50%
    72	            of the width, the chat history on the right taking the rest. The
    73	            split can be resized by dragging its edge. Closing the file closes
    74	            the split.
    75	
    76	            When the split opens, it slides in from the sidebar, so it's clear
    77	            where it came from: the file's side grows out of the sidebar's edge
    78	            to its share of the width, the file sliding into view from behind
    79	            that edge as it does, while the chat history gives way beside it.
    80	            The slide is quick and settles without bouncing, and only then can
    81	            the split be dragged. A file opened in place of one already showing
    82	            doesn't slide, since the split is already open. The
    83	            @{ChatInputScope} is never split: it stays along the bottom, across
    84	            the full width of prompt mode.
    85	
    86	            Closing the file plays the slide in reverse, back into the
    87	            sidebar: the file's side shrinks from whatever width it was
    88	            dragged to down to nothing at the sidebar's edge, the file sliding
    89	            out of view behind that edge as it does, while the chat history
    90	            grows back across the full width. It is as quick as the slide in,
    91	            and settles without bouncing. Opening a file while one is still
    92	            sliding out slides the new one in straight away.
    93	
    94	        openDiff:
    95	            A file's @{DiffViewScope}, opened from the @{FileTreeScope}, opens
    96	            in an @{InsetPanelScope}. It leaves the split alone: any file open
    97	            there stays open, unsaved changes and all. Opening another file's
    98	            diff replaces the one in the panel, as does opening one while a new
    99	            project is being set up. Opening the file from the diff closes the
   100	            panel and opens the file in the split, as clicking it in the
   101	            @{FileTreeScope} would.
   102	
   103	        analyzeDivergence:
   104	            The ribbon's Analyze Divergence command opens the @{DivergenceScope}
   105	            in an @{InsetPanelScope}, to analyze, in place of whatever else is
   106	            open there, or brings back one that was minimized.
   107	
   108	        rescope:
   109	            The ribbon's Rescope command opens the @{RescopeScope} in an
   110	            @{InsetPanelScope}, in place of whatever else is open there, or
   111	            brings back one that was minimized. Its Refactor sends its prompt as
   112	            if from the chat input's Spec tab.
   113	
   114	        viewDivergenceReports:
   115	            The ribbon's View Divergence Reports command opens the
   116	            @{DivergenceScope} the same way, to view the reports, without
   117	            starting an analysis.
   118	
   119	        newProject:
   120	            The ribbon's New Project command opens the @{NewProjectScope} in an
   121	            @{InsetPanelScope}, fresh each time, in place of any diff open
   122	            there. Once the project is created, the panel closes and the new
   123	            project is open.
   124	
   125	        openProject:
   126	            The Open Project commands, from the ribbon or the palette, show the
   127	            @{OpenProjectScope} in an @{InsetPanelScope}, in place of whatever
   128	            else is open there.
   129	
   130	        settings:
   131	            The settings, opened with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS), the ribbon's
   132	            Settings command, or the palette, show the @{SettingsWindowScope}
   133	            in an @{InsetPanelScope}, in place of whatever else is open there.
   134	
   135	        promptMode:
   136	            The body displays the @{PromptEditor} and any splits, to the right
   137	            of the @{SidebarScope}.
=== spec/scope/palette/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /scope/project/open-project import OpenProjectScope
     3	from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
     4	from /scope/project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     5	from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
     6	from /scope/editor import EditorScope
     7	from /ui/components/file-tree import FileTreeScope
     8	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
     9	from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
    10	from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
    11	
    12	export scope PaletteScope:
    13	    concept: {PaletteConcept}
    14	
    15	concept PaletteConcept:
    16	    pitch:
    17	        A popover for finding anything in the application by fuzzy searching
    18	        for it: the project's files, the application's own commands, and the
    19	        harness's commands, skills, and agents.
    20	
    21	    shape: {PaletteShape}
    22	
    23	shape PaletteShape:
    24	    description:
    25	        A popover near the top of the window, over a dimmed backdrop: a tab bar
    26	        using gpui-kit's default tab styling, a search field beneath it, and the
    27	        results beneath that.
    28	
    29	    opening:
    30	        Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on macOS) anywhere in the window opens the palette on the
    31	        Files tab with an empty search and focus in the search field. Pressing
    32	        it again while the palette is open closes it.
    33	
    34	    closing:
    35	        Picking a result closes the palette. Esc clears the search, and closes
    36	        the palette once the search is empty. Clicking outside the palette
    37	        closes it. Closing it without picking anything puts focus back where it
    38	        was.
    39	
    40	    tabs:
    41	        overview:
    42	            The tabs are Files, System, Commands, Skills, and Agents, in that
    43	            order. Each lists its own results. The search is kept when switching
    44	            tabs, and applies to the tab switched to.
    45	
    46	        switching:
    47	            Clicking a tab switches to it. <Tab> moves to the next tab and
    48	            <Shift+Tab> to the previous one, wrapping around, and focus stays in
    49	            the search field.
    50	
    51	        files:
    52	            Every file in the selected @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, at any depth,
    53	            listed by its path in the project. `.git`, and whatever the
    54	            project's `.gitignore` files ignore, are left out. Picking a file
    55	            opens it in the @{EditorScope}, as clicking it in the
    56	            @{FileTreeScope} does. Until a project is picked the tab reads
    57	            "No project open".
    58	
    59	        fileSearch:
    60	            On the Files tab, Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) sends the search
    61	            to a separate harness run that finds the file being described, even
    62	            when files match. Plain Enter does the same once the file list has
    63	            loaded and nothing matches; otherwise it picks the highlighted file.
    64	            While nothing matches, the results area says so and how to search
    65	            with the harness instead, reading
    66	            "No results. Press Enter to perform an agentic search." in place of
    67	            "No matches".
    68	            While the search runs, the results area shows its task table, as in
    69	            the @{MessageList}, scrolling with a @{ScrollbarScope}. When it
    70	            finishes, a single file closes the palette and opens that file,
    71	            several files show a "Multiple results were found" alert, and no
    72	            files adds a "No file matching the search was found." row. Changing
    73	            the search or switching tabs stops the run and brings back the
    74	            normal results, and if the palette closes while it runs, nothing
    75	            opens.
    76	
    77	        fileSearchSystemPrompt:
    78	            The search's system prompt, system-prompts/file-search.pi, built
    79	            into the application (see @{HarnessIntegrationScope}), is appended
    80	            to the harness's own. It tells the harness we're really trying to find the one file being
    81	            asked for, giving several only when they are all equally what was
    82	            asked for; to only read and never change anything; and to stop as
    83	            soon as it is confident. It lists where to look, in this order of
    84	            priority, preferring a match from an earlier place over an equally
    85	            good match from a later one: the spec, at `root` in piton.config.pi;
    86	            the code, at `codeRoot` in piton.config.pi; `.suspense`; then
    87	            `.claude`. A location missing from the config is left out of the
    88	            list. The harness's final reply is only JSON listing the files by
    89	            path relative to the project, and paths that don't exist are
    90	            dropped.
    91	
    92	        system:
    93	            The application's own commands, each doing what its toolbar control
    94	            or shortcut does: "Open Project…", which opens the
    95	            @{OpenProjectScope}, "Build", "Dark mode" or
    96	            "Light mode" (whichever is not the current one), "Settings…", which
    97	            opens the @{SettingsWindowScope}, and "Quit". Build is unavailable
    98	            while there is no project or a build is running.
    99	
   100	        commands:
   101	            The harness's commands, the same ones the @{ChatInputScope} offers
   102	            after `/`.
   103	
   104	        skills:
   105	            The harness's skills, the same ones the @{ChatInputScope} offers
   106	            after `/`.
   107	
   108	        agents:
   109	            The harness's agents, the same ones the @{ChatInputScope} offers
   110	            after `@`.
   111	
   112	        mentions:
   113	            A command, skill, or agent shows its description when it has one.
   114	            Picking one inserts it into the @{ChatInputScope} at the cursor the
   115	            way accepting it as a mention does, `/name ` for a command or skill
   116	            and `@agent-name ` for an agent, with a space before it when the
   117	            cursor follows other text. Focus then moves to the chat input.
   118	
   119	    fuzzySearch:
   120	        A result matches when the search's characters all appear in it in order,
   121	        ignoring case, though not necessarily next to each other. The best
   122	        matches come first: runs of consecutive characters, and characters at
   123	        the start of a word or of a file's name, rank higher, then shorter
   124	        results. The matched characters are highlighted. With an empty search,
   125	        files are listed by path, the application's commands in the order above,
   126	        and the harness's by name. At most the 100 best results are listed.
   127	
   128	    keyboard:
   129	        Up and Down move the highlight, which starts on the first result, and
   130	        Enter picks the highlighted result. Clicking a result picks it.
=== spec/scope/harness-integration/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     3	from ../settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
     4	
     5	export scope HarnessIntegrationScope:
     6	    concept: {HarnessIntegrationConcept}
     7	
     8	concept HarnessIntegrationConcept:
     9	    pitch:
    10	        Uses the one-off version for a coding harness for the selected
    11	        ${ProjectDirectoryScope}. For example, `claude -p`. Each run carries on
    12	        a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.
    13	
    14	    shape: {HarnessIntegrationShape}
    15	
    16	shape HarnessIntegrationShape:
    17	    description:
    18	        Should always run in auto mode.
    19	
    20	        The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor is appended to
    21	        the harness's own system prompt, for example with
    22	        `--append-system-prompt`.
    23	
    24	        The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the
    25	        harness does is streamed back as it happens.
    26	
    27	    context:
    28	        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting
    29	        fresh each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task
    30	        sent carries it on. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the
    31	        latest conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a
    32	        separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they
    33	        carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of
    34	        that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write
    35	        over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in,
    36	        and if one can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each
    37	        run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a
    38	        conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search
    39	        always starts fresh.
    40	
    41	    bakedPrompts:
    42	        The prompts the application gives the harness for its own work, rather
    43	        than a prompt someone writes, are Piton files in the repository's
    44	        system-prompts folder, one for each:
    45	        - divergence.pi, for the two agents of a divergence analysis
    46	        - commit-note.pi, for a finished task's commit note
    47	        - commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
    48	        - file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description
    49	
    50	        Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for
    51	        each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a
    52	        heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a
    53	        name in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.
    54	
    55	        They are compiled with `piton compile` when the application is built,
    56	        and built into it: changing one changes what the next build sends, and
    57	        a prompt that doesn't compile fails the build, with piton's error. Each
    58	        build keeps what it compiled in system-prompts/compiled.json, with the
    59	        source, so the application still builds where `piton` isn't installed,
    60	        such as on CI, from the prompts as last compiled, saying so.
    61	
    62	        The per-mode system prompt templates are separate: they are saved with
    63	        each project, in its .suspense/system-prompts, and edited in the
    64	        @{SettingsWindowScope}.
=== spec/scope/settings-window/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     3	from ../prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
     4	from /ui/components/inset-panel import InsetPanelScope
     5	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
     6	
     7	export scope SettingsWindowScope:
     8	    concept: {SettingsWindowConcept}
     9	
    10	concept SettingsWindowConcept:
    11	    pitch:
    12	        The application's settings, which for now are
    13	        the system prompts each tab of the @{ChatInputScope} sends.
    14	
    15	    shape: {SettingsWindowShape}
    16	
    17	shape SettingsWindowShape:
    18	    description:
    19	        Shown in an @{InsetPanelScope} over the main window, not a window of its
    20	        own. It is headed "Settings", with a close button whose tooltip says it
    21	        closes the settings; closing the panel any way an inset panel closes
    22	        closes them too. Beneath the heading, its page scrolls with a
    23	        @{ScrollbarScope}.
    24	
    25	    opening:
    26	        It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application,
    27	        or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else
    28	        in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it
    29	        is rather than opening another.
    30	
    31	    systemPrompts:
    32	        The page is headed "System prompts", with a muted line beneath saying
    33	        that each tab gives a prompt sent from it this system prompt, that they
    34	        are saved with the project as they are edited, and that the
    35	        CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION placeholders stand for codeRoot and root
    36	        in piton.config.pi.
    37	
    38	        Then, for each tab in order, Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask: its name, the
    39	        muted path of the file its prompt is saved in, and a "Reset to default"
    40	        button, disabled while the prompt is already the default, which puts the
    41	        default back and saves it. Beneath them, an editor for the prompt, 120
    42	        pixels tall before it scrolls, highlighting it as Piton, with soft
    43	        wrapping and no line numbers or folding. A prompt that can't be read or
    44	        saved says why beneath its editor.
    45	
    46	        Without a project open, in place of the prompts it reads
    47	        "Open a project to edit its system prompts."
    48	
    49	    saving:
    50	        The prompts belong to the project opened through the
    51	        @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, each saved as a Markdown file named after its
    52	        tab in the project's `.suspense/system-prompts` directory. Every edit is
    53	        saved straight away. When the window loads the prompts, any tab with no
    54	        file yet has its default saved, so every prompt can also be found and
    55	        edited by hand. The prompts are read again each time the settings open
    56	        and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows
    57	        up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its
    58	        cursor stays put.
    59	
    60	    templates:
    61	        A prompt is a template: the placeholders CODE_LOCATION and
    62	        SPEC_LOCATION, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a
    63	        Piton interpolation, are filled in with codeRoot and root from the
    64	        project's piton.config.pi before the prompt is compiled. Otherwise it is
    65	        Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can reference the
    66	        spec. The defaults, which a reset puts back, are the ones the
    67	        @{ChatInputScope} gives each tab, baked into the application when it is
    68	        built.

    10	        Uses the one-off version for a coding harness for the selected

    12	        a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

    17	    description:
    18	        Should always run in auto mode.
    19	
    20	        The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor is appended to
    21	        the harness's own system prompt, for example with
    22	        `--append-system-prompt`.
    23	
    24	        The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the
    25	        harness does is streamed back as it happens.
    26	
    27	    context:
    28	        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting
    29	        fresh each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task
    30	        sent carries it on. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the
    31	        latest conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a
    32	        separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they
    33	        carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of
    34	        that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write
    35	        over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in,
    36	        and if one can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each
    37	        run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a
    38	        conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search

    49	
    50	        Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for
    51	        each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a
    52	        heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a
    53	        name in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.

=== spec/ui/components/git-panel/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope

     6	
     7	export scope GitPanelScope:
     8	    concept: {GitPanelConcept}
     9	
    10	concept GitPanelConcept:
    11	    pitch:
    12	        A very basic git panel for the repository the
    13	        ${ProjectDirectoryScope} is in, as the @{GitScope} knows it: see what
    14	        has changed at a glance, write a commit message, commit, push, and
    15	        pull.
    16	
    17	    shape: {GitPanelShape}
    18	
    19	shape GitPanelShape:
    20	    description:
    21	        A compact panel with a thin border along its top. It is shown only
    22	        while the project is inside a git repository.
    23	
    24	    branch:
    25	        The top row shows the branch from the @{GitScope}, or
    26	        "Detached HEAD", beside how many commits it is ahead of its upstream
    27	        (↑) and behind it (↓), each only when not zero. At the right end are a Pull button and a Push
    28	        button, icons with tooltips.
    29	
    30	    summary:
    31	        Below the branch, a line counts the @{GitScope}'s changes, leaving out
    32	        any kind with none, as "2 modified · 1 untracked", or "No changes".
    33	        Beside it, how many lines were added (+, in green) and removed (−, in
    34	        red). The files themselves are not listed, since the @{FileTreeScope}
    35	        shows them. The summary refreshes as the @{GitScope} does, and
    36	        straight after anything the panel does.
    37	
    38	    commitNotes:
    39	        Above the message box, a row for each commit note, in the order they
    40	        were added: a one-line box holding the note, which can be edited, and a
    41	        small button to remove it. Each Code, Chain, or Spec task that finishes
    42	        without error adds a note, a one-line summary of what the task changed,
    43	        once the harness has written it, quickly, in the same way as a written
    44	        message: from what the task asked and the harness's own summary of what
    45	        it did, at most 72 characters in the imperative mood, as
    46	        system-prompts/commit-note.pi asks. A task that
    47	        changed no files adds none, and neither does a question from the Ask
    48	        tab. Notes are saved with the project, in its
    49	        `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, as they are added, edited, and removed,
    50	        so they survive a restart; that file is never itself committed.
    51	
    52	    message:
    53	        A commit message box, a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 10 rows at
    54	        most, so it starts at a single row. It reads "Commit message" while
    55	        empty.
    56	
    57	    writingAMessage:
    58	        A "Write message" button, with a sparkles icon, has the harness write
    59	        the commit message from what has changed, and puts it in the message
    60	        box, replacing what was there. It is quick: a small, fast model, at
    61	        low effort, with no tools, handed only the list of changed files and
    62	        as much of the diff as fits in a small, fixed amount. The message is a
    63	        summary line of at most 72 characters in the imperative mood,
    64	        followed, only if it helps, by a few short bullet points, as
    65	        system-prompts/commit-message.pi asks. The button
    66	        is disabled while there are no changes.
    67	
    68	    committing:
    69	        A primary "Commit" button commits every change, new files included.
    70	        The commit message is what was typed, then a blank line, then each
    71	        note that isn't blank as a line of its own starting "- "; with nothing
    72	        typed, it is the notes alone. Once committed, the message box and the
    73	        notes are cleared. It is disabled while there is neither a message nor
    74	        a note, or there are no changes.
    75	
    76	    pushingAndPulling:
    77	        Push pushes the branch, setting its upstream on origin first if it has
    78	        none.
    79	
    80	        Pull fetches the branch's upstream. With nothing new it says the
    81	        branch is already up to date. When only the upstream has moved on, the
    82	        branch fast-forwards to it. When both have moved on, the upstream is
    83	        merged in automatically, as long as the merge has no conflicts. If it
    84	        would conflict, the pull is cancelled before anything changes: the
    85	        branch, its files, and the index stay exactly as they were, no merge is
    86	        left in progress, and an error names the files that would have
    87	        conflicted. Pull is disabled while the branch has no upstream.
    88	
    89	    feedback:
    90	        While the panel is committing, pushing, pulling, or writing a
    91	        message, that button shows a spinner and the others are disabled.
    92	        Committing, pushing, and pulling say so in a notification when they
    93	        succeed; a pull says whether it was already up to date, pulled, or
    94	        pulled and merged. Anything that fails says why in an error notification.

     1	use /lib

     4	
     5	export scope DiffViewScope:
     6	    concept: {DiffViewConcept}
     7	
     8	concept DiffViewConcept:
     9	    pitch:
    10	        A view of one file's uncommitted changes: the file as of the last
    11	        commit, from the @{GitScope}, against the file as it is on disk.
    12	
    13	    shape: {DiffViewShape}
    14	
    15	shape DiffViewShape:
    16	    description:
    17	        A header along the top, and beneath it the changes, which scroll with
    18	        a @{ScrollbarScope}. It fills whatever holds it, and follows the
    19	        file as it changes on disk.
    20	
    21	    header:
    22	        The file's path in the project, beside a diff icon, and how many lines
    23	        were added (+, in green) and removed (−, in red). At the right end:
    24	        buttons to step to the previous and next change; a switch between
    25	        "Side by side" and "Unified", each with an icon, the chosen one shown
    26	        selected; a button that opens the file in the editor instead; and a
    27	        close button.
    28	
    29	    layouts:
    30	        sideBySide:
    31	            The file as of the last commit on the left and as it is now on the
    32	            right, divided by a thin line. A removed line faces the added line
    33	            that replaced it, and a line with no counterpart faces blank,
    34	            shaded filler, so the two sides stay level. Each side has its own
    35	            line numbers.
    36	
    37	        unified:
    38	            One column, with each block of removed lines before the added
    39	            lines that replaced them. Each line shows both line numbers: its
    40	            number in the old file and in the new, either blank where the line
    41	            isn't in that version.
    42	
    43	        The chosen layout is remembered for the user across launches; it
    44	        starts side by side.
    45	
    46	    lines:
    47	        Lines are shown in the editor's monospace font, one row each, without
    48	        wrapping, tabs shown as four spaces. An added line is tinted green and
    49	        marked +, a removed line tinted red and marked −, so a change never
    50	        relies on colour alone; unchanged lines are neither. Within a line
    51	        that replaced, or was replaced by, a similar one, the words that
    52	        changed get a stronger tint of the same colour. A line changed through
    53	        and through isn't marked word by word.
    54	
    55	    unchangedLines:
    56	        Three unchanged lines are kept either side of each change. A longer run
    57	        of unchanged lines, four or more, collapses into a single shaded row
    58	        reading "Show N unchanged lines", which expands them when clicked. A
    59	        file with no changes is shown whole.
    60	
    61	    navigating:
    62	        F7 steps to the next change and Shift+F7 to the previous one, stopping
    63	        at the first and last, as do the header's buttons. The change stepped
    64	        to is scrolled to the middle of the view and marked with an accent bar
    65	        along its left.
    66	
    67	    states:
    68	        While the file is read it says "Loading…". A binary file says its
    69	        changes can't be shown. An empty file says so. A file that can't be
    70	        read says why.

2	     1	use /lib
3	     2	from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
4	     3	from /ui/components/selection-popover import SelectionPopoverScope
5	     4	from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope

12	    11	
13	    12	export scope ChatInputScope:
14	    13	    concept: {ChatInputConcept}
15	    14	
16	    15	concept ChatInputConcept:
17	    16	    pitch:
18	    17	        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
19	    18	        as snippets of Piton.
20	    19	
21	    20	    shape: {ChatInputShape}
22	    21	
23	    22	shape ChatInputShape:
24	    23	    description:
25	    24	        Input on the left, send button on the right.
26	    25	
27	    26	        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
28	    27	        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}
29	    28	
30	    29	        Sending is never blocked by the harness working: while it is, the send
31	    30	        button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue" and sending adds
32	    31	        the prompt to prompt mode's queue. On the Ask tab it always reads
33	    32	        "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled
34	    33	        while the input is empty.
35	    34	
36	    35	    tabs:
37	    36	        overview:
38	    37	            The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using
39	    38	            gpui-kit's default tab styling. There are four tabs, in order: Code,
40	    39	            Chain, Spec, and Ask. Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain
41	    40	            is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All
42	    41	            four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has
43	    42	            more padding than a normal tab.
44	    43	
45	    44	            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
46	    45	            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
47	    46	            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
48	    47	
49	    48	            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
50	    49	            Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
51	    50	            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
52	    51	            not <Cmd>.
53	    52	
54	    53	            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
55	    54	            either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
56	    55	            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
57	    56	            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.
58	    57	
59	    58	        chain:
60	    59	            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
61	    60	            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
62	    61	            selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its
63	    62	            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
64	    63	            is selected.
65	    64	
66	    65	            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
67	    66	            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
68	    67	            them.
69	    68	
70	    69	            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
71	    70	            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
72	    71	            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
73	    72	            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
74	    73	            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
75	    74	            Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified
76	    75	            tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent
77	    76	            background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec
78	    77	            show through underneath it.
79	    78	
80	    79	        help:
81	    80	            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
82	    81	            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
83	    82	            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
84	    83	            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
85	    84	            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
86	    85	            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
87	    86	
88	    87	            code:
89	    88	                Changes the code, leaving the spec as it is.
90	    89	
91	    90	            chain:
92	    91	                Changes the code and the spec together.
93	    92	
94	    93	            spec:

100	    99	        colour:

102	   101	            subtle red for Code, a subtle blue for Spec, and a subtle green for
103	   102	            Ask. With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple.
104	   103	            The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes,
105	   104	            straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap
106	   105	            around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's
107	   106	            red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green;
108	   107	            neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.
109	   108	
110	   109	    systemPrompt:
111	   110	        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode gives
112	   111	        the hidden anchor a systemPrompt property alongside its userPrompt. The
113	   112	        code location is `codeRoot` and the spec location is `root`, as set in
114	   113	        the project's piton.config.pi.
115	   114	
116	   115	        defaults:
117	   116	            Each mode's default system prompt is the template saved for it in
118	   117	            this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts`
119	   118	            directory, one Markdown file per mode: code.md, combined.md for
120	   119	            Chain, spec.md, and ask.md. They are the source of truth for the
121	   120	            defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a
122	   121	            build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them
123	   122	            changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
124	   123	            without them.
125	   124	
126	   125	            The defaults are only where a project starts: each is saved with the
127	   126	            project and can be edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}.
128	   127	
129	   128	        A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.
130	   129	
131	   130	    ask:
132	   131	        Ask is for simply asking a question. A question runs straight away,
133	   132	        separately from any Code, Chain, or Spec task, even while the harness is
134	   133	        working on one. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run
135	   134	        at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already
136	   135	        running.
137	   136	
138	   137	        Each question's progress and results are shown in a task table, as in
139	   138	        the @{MessageList}. The questions stack directly above the tabs, the
140	   139	        newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make
141	   140	        room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is
142	   141	        ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an
143	   142	        animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While
144	   143	        the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest
145	   144	        thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and
146	   145	        first line.
147	   146	
148	   147	        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
149	   148	        and first line, above its full task table, in the answer drawer, which
150	   149	        it fills, scrolling once it is taller, with a @{ScrollbarScope} and its
151	   150	        lock to the bottom. Only one question is open at a time: opening another
152	   151	        closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the
153	   152	        stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down
154	   153	        to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it
155	   154	        again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it
156	   155	        if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question
157	   156	        becomes a previous answer.
158	   157	
159	   158	    answerSteps:
160	   159	        For a question, only the answer matters, so the steps leading up to it
161	   160	        are collapsed by default wherever a finished question's task table
162	   161	        is shown: an open question, and a previous answer. The steps are every
163	   162	        row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the
164	   163	        rows after it. In their place, the table's first row reads "Show 1 step"
165	   164	        or "Show N steps", muted, beside a right chevron, with the answer
166	   165	        beneath it. A single click on that row expands the steps in place, above
167	   166	        the answer, and the row then reads "Hide 1 step" or "Hide N steps"
168	   167	        beside a down chevron; clicking it again collapses them. Each question's
169	   168	        table is expanded or collapsed on its own, and a question closed into
170	   169	        the previous answers starts collapsed again.
171	   170	
172	   171	        A reply with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has
173	   172	        nothing to collapse and shows whole. A question still running shows its
174	   173	        latest step as usual. Tasks are never collapsed like this, since their
175	   174	        whole chain is of interest: see the @{MessageList}.
176	   175	
177	   176	    previousAnswers:
178	   177	        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
179	   178	        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
180	   179	        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
181	   180	        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
182	   181	        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
183	   182	        "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the
184	   183	        answer drawer, the list sliding up from on top of any question rows
185	   184	        still in the stack, rather than out of the chat input over them: those
186	   185	        rows stay where they were, in view and undimmed, beneath the drawer, and
187	   186	        with no rows left there it slides up out of the chat input as usual. The
188	   187	        questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them
189	   188	        left off.
190	   189	
191	   190	    answerDrawer:
192	   191	        Only a question open onto its task table, or the previous answers
193	   192	        expanded, are a drawer. Unlike the stack of question rows, which pushes
194	   193	        what is above it, the drawer slides up out of the chat input over
195	   194	        everything above it, the message list, any file beside it, and the
196	   195	        stack, covering them rather than pushing them, and dims them: see the
197	   196	        @{MessageList}. The previous answers are the exception: they slide up
198	   197	        from on top of the question rows in the stack, leaving those rows
199	   198	        uncovered and undimmed, and the drawer's share of the space counts from
200	   199	        the chat input, rows included. Closing it slides nothing back; the stack
201	   200	        and the message list are where they were beneath it.
202	   201	
203	   202	        The drawer opens to 80% of the height of the space above the chat input
204	   203	        by default: the open question's table, or the previous answers list,
205	   204	        grows to fill whatever the drawer's other rows leave, rather than
206	   205	        stopping at a fixed height. It slides up out of the chat input as it
207	   206	        opens.
208	   207	
209	   208	        While open, the drawer is resizable by dragging its top edge, which
210	   209	        shows a resize cursor and a thin highlight when hovered. It follows the
211	   210	        pointer exactly, with no slide, and can be dragged from 20% to 95% of
212	   211	        that space. The size it is dragged to is kept for as long as the
213	   212	        application runs, for every question or list opened afterwards, rather
214	   213	        than going back to 80%.
215	   214	
216	   215	    selectingAnswerText:
217	   216	        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
218	   217	        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
219	   218	        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
220	   219	        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
221	   220	        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
222	   221	
223	   222	        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
224	   223	        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
225	   224	        popover also closes when the drawer closes.
226	   225	
227	   226	    attachments:
228	   227	        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
229	   228	        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
230	   229	        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
231	   230	        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
232	   231	        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
233	   232	        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
234	   233	        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
235	   234	
236	   235	        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
237	   236	        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
238	   237	        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
239	   238	        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
240	   239	        the attachments it was sent with.
241	   240	
242	   241	    escape:
243	   242	        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
244	   243	        input.

249	   248	
250	   249	    autoFocus:

252	   251	
253	   252	    syntaxHighlighting:

257	   256	    lsp: @{LSP}
258	   257	
259	   258	    harnessMentions:
260	   259	        overview:
261	   260	            Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@`
262	   261	            offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself.
263	   262	            The placeholder mentions both.
264	   263	
265	   264	        trigger:
266	   265	            A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after
267	   266	            whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at
268	   267	            sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference.
269	   268	            Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after
270	   269	            each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that
271	   270	            follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger;
272	   271	            outside of one they never reach the @{LSP}.
273	   272	
274	   273	        offered:
275	   274	            Skills and commands are those of the selected
276	   275	            ${ProjectDirectoryScope}, of the user, and of the user's enabled
277	   276	            plugins, a plugin's own being named `plugin:name`. Agents come from
278	   277	            the same places, plus the harness's built-in agents. Each shows
279	   278	            whether it is a skill, command, or agent, and its description as
280	   279	            documentation when it has one. Every harness run reports the skills
281	   280	            and agents it has, built-in ones included; the last report is saved
282	   281	            with the project and offered too. Results are narrowed and ordered
283	   282	            like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before
284	   283	            matches anywhere in it, then by name.
285	   284	
286	   285	        accepting:
287	   286	            Accepting a skill or command inserts `/name `, and accepting an
288	   287	            agent inserts `@agent-name `, which the harness understands as a
289	   288	            request to use that agent. They pass through the hidden anchor and
290	   289	            its compilation unchanged, so a prompt starting with `/name` runs
291	   290	            that skill or command. Mentions work without the @{LSP}.
292	   291	
293	   292	    hiddenAnchor:
294	   293	        While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes,
295	   294	        they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt
296	   295	        property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the
297	   296	        @{HarnessIntegrationScope}
298	   297	
299	   298	        escaping:
300	   299	            A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it
301	   300	            isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, quotes,
302	   301	            colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and
303	   302	            backslashes all mean something. Its userPrompt is a list with an
304	   303	            item per line of the prompt, in order, and each line a list of its
305	   304	            pieces: the text between references as a quoted string, with
306	   305	            quotes, backslashes, and each dollar-brace escaped, so nothing in it
307	   306	            is interpolated or evaluated; and each at-brace or dollar-brace
308	   307	            around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported as
309	   308	            a reference of its own. A reference to a name that isn't imported,
310	   309	            such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. An empty line is a
311	   310	            single empty string. The compiled userPrompt is the pieces of each
312	   311	            line joined together, and the lines joined by line breaks, so what
313	   312	            the harness receives is exactly what was typed or pasted, line for
314	   313	            line, with each reference resolved. The systemPrompt is written the
315	   314	            same way. A prompt saved as prose by an earlier version still reads
316	   315	            back.
317	   316	
318	   317	        autoImports:
319	   318	            The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there,
320	   319	            typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the
321	   320	            prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position
322	   321	            for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other
323	   322	            than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out,
324	   323	            character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or
325	   324	            brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment
326	   325	            then never stops the server finding the names that need importing,
327	   326	            both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.
328	   327	
329	   328	        attachedText:
330	   329	            A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText
331	   330	            property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the
332	   331	            order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not
333	   332	            as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a
334	   333	            quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it
335	   334	            is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no
336	   335	            attachedText property.
337	   336	
338	   337	            What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the
339	   338	            attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a
340	   339	            fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks
341	   340	            in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the
342	   341	            task's header.

354	    11	concept PromptEditorConcept:
355	    12	    pitch:
356	    13	        An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude
357	    14	        Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.
358	    15	
359	    16	    shape: {PromptEditorShape}
360	    17	
361	    18	shape PromptEditorShape:
362	    19	    description:
363	    20	        Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can
364	    21	        queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no
365	    22	        message bubbles.
366	    23	
367	    24	    basicDesignAndLayout:
368	    25	        The @{MessageList} fills all available space except for a
369	    26	        @{ChatInputScope} along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the
370	    27	        previous tasks row, the header for the latest task, the latest task's
371	    28	        output, and the queue.
372	    29	
373	    30	        Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which
374	    31	        wraps when the view is narrow. It reads
375	    32	        "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it."
376	    33	        or, while no project is open, "Open a project to start prompting."
377	    34	
378	    35	    chatHistory: @{MessageList}
379	    36	
380	    37	    previousTasks:
381	    38	        Previous tasks are a @{HistoryListScope} along the top of the view,
382	    39	        listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but the latest,
383	    40	        which heads the view: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or
384	    41	        "N previous tasks". Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest
385	    42	        task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".
386	    43	
387	    44	    header:
388	    45	        The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working:
389	    46	        its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the
390	    47	        hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the
391	    48	        harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it
392	    49	        has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead.
393	    50	
394	    51	    queue:
395	    52	        overview:
396	    53	            Prompts can still be sent while the harness is working: they wait
397	    54	            in a queue, in the order they were sent, and are sent one at a
398	    55	            time. While the harness is working, the chat input's send button
399	    56	            reads "Queue".
400	    57	
401	    58	            A question from the Ask tab never queues. It runs straight away,
402	    59	            even while the harness is working on a task.
403	    60	
404	    61	        placement:
405	    62	            The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and
406	    63	            directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is
407	    64	            not part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued,
408	    65	            with a chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line
409	    66	            or two of each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list
410	    67	            is numbered, with its number, text, and cancel button vertically
411	    68	            centred in its row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a
412	    69	            @{ScrollbarScope}. Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to
413	    70	            the bottom, on the prompts queued most recently, however it was
414	    71	            scrolled when last closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch
415	    72	            and the "Send next" button.
416	    73	            The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.
417	    74	
418	    75	        cancel:
419	    76	            A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which
420	    77	            removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no
421	    78	            longer in the queue.
422	    79	
423	    80	        autoSend:
424	    81	            A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending the next
425	    82	            queued prompt as soon as the harness is free, and waiting. It starts
426	    83	            switched on. Switching it on while the harness is free sends the
427	    84	            next queued prompt straight away. Whenever the harness is free and
428	    85	            the queue is not empty, a "Send next" button sends the first queued
429	    86	            prompt. A prompt that fails to compile or run does not stop the
430	    87	            queue.
431	    88	
432	    89	        persistence:
433	    90	            Queued prompts are saved in the project's `.suspense/queue`
434	    91	            directory, each as its hidden anchor's source, imports included,
435	    92	            the way prompt history is, and named so they list in the order they
436	    93	            were queued. The queue is restored whenever the project is opened;
437	    94	            a restored queue waits for "Send next" rather than sending on its
438	    95	            own. A queued prompt's file is removed when it is cancelled, or
439	    96	            when it is sent, at which point it is saved to the prompt history
440	    97	            like any other prompt.
441	    98	
442	    99	    buildingTheSpec:
443	   100	        Before a Code, Chain, or Spec prompt is sent, `piton build` runs in the
444	   101	        project, so the compiled spec the harness reads is up to date. It runs
445	   102	        when the prompt is actually sent, so a queued prompt builds when its
446	   103	        turn comes, not when it is queued. The task shows "Building" until the
447	   104	        build is over. A build that fails does not stop the prompt, since the
448	   105	        prompt may be the one to fix the spec: the task's output starts with
449	   106	        an error saying the build failed, so the compiled spec may be out of
450	   107	        date, with what the build reported. A question from the Ask tab is sent
451	   108	        without building.
452	   109	
453	   110	    commitNote:
454	   111	        Once a Code, Chain, or Spec task finishes without error, it adds a
455	   112	        commit note summarising what it changed to the @{GitPanelScope}.
456	   113	
457	   114	    history:
458	   115	        Every task sent is saved in the project's `.suspense/history` directory
459	   116	        as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the
460	   117	        anchor's name. Once its run is over, what came of it is saved beside it
461	   118	        in a `.json` file of the same name: the compiled userPrompt the harness
462	   119	        received, each line the harness printed, and any error. Opening the
463	   120	        project brings back every task in order, with its output replayed from
464	   121	        that record. A task with no record shows as "Not recorded".
465	   122	
466	   123	        Every question asked from the Ask tab is logged the same way, but in
467	   124	        the project's `.suspense/asks` directory instead, so it never comes back
468	   125	        as a task: its hidden anchor's source, and beside it a `.json` record
469	   126	        of what came of it. The record is saved when the run is over, and also
470	   127	        when the question is closed or replaced while it runs, with as much as
471	   128	        the harness had done. A question that fails before it reaches the
472	   129	        harness is logged too, with the error in its record.

493	    18	        Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown
494	    19	        on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered

501	    26

505	    30	        "Failed" in red, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history

534	    59	        Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the
535	    60	        project directory itself reads `.`.
536	    61	
537	    62	        A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long
538	    63	        one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per
539	    64	        line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes,
540	    65	        command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs. Other arguments
541	    66	        are shown on a single line.
542	    67	
543	    68	    running:
544	    69	        While a task is under way, its table ends in a row for whatever the
545	    70	        harness does next. Until a row has something meaningful to show, its
546	    71	        Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last three lines
547	    72	        of the harness's raw output: muted, monospace, JSON syntax-highlighted,
548	    73	        and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump. Before any output
549	    74	        has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…". As soon as a row's type
550	    75	        is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its text or argument
551	    76	        arrives, that is shown. While the input of a Files, Edit, Command, Web,
552	    77	        or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell shows only a skeleton.
553	    78	
554	    79	    runningSkeleton:
555	    80	        A skeleton stands in for a currently running task only while there is
556	    81	        nothing meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is anything
557	    82	        meaningful to display for that task in the message list, no skeleton is
558	    83	        shown for it at all.
559	    84	
560	    85	    links:
561	    86	        Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to
562	    87	        a file opens it in the @{EditorScope} beside the task view, a web link
563	    88	        opens in the browser, and a link to a file that doesn't exist shows an
564	    89	        error notification. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit
565	    90	        row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.
566	    91	
567	    92	    backgrounds:
568	    93	        The header for the latest task is coloured like the tab the task was
569	    94	        sent from, the same colour the @{ChatInputScope} body shows for that
570	    95	        tab: a subtle red for Code, purple for Chain, and a subtle blue for
571	    96	        Spec. A task from the history that doesn't say which tab it was sent
572	    97	        from keeps the tab bar's colour. The queue along the bottom and the
573	    98	        previous tasks row along the top both have the same background colour as
574	    99	        the tab bar.
575	   100	
576	   101	    askDimming:
577	   102	        While a finished question from the Ask tab is open onto its full task
578	   103	        table, a dark shade fades in over the message list to draw attention to
579	   104	        it, and fades back out when it is closed or closed down to its row. The
580	   105	        shade also shows while the previous answers are expanded on the Ask
581	   106	        tab: while the answer drawer is open. Question rows in the stack above
582	   107	        the tabs, running or finished, never dim the list; they push it up
583	   108	        instead. The shade covers all the space above the chat input beneath the
584	   109	        drawer: the message list, any file open beside it, and the stack of
585	   110	        question rows.
586	   111	
587	   112	    scrolling:
588	   113	        The latest task's output scrolls with a @{ScrollbarScope}, with its
589	   114	        lock to the bottom. Unlocked, it still follows new output while it is
590	   115	        already scrolled to the bottom. The lock is off until switched on.
591	   116	
592	   117	        The rows of the output table scroll beneath its header, which stays at
593	   118	        the top. However long the output or the list of previous tasks grows,
594	   119	        drawing it costs no more than drawing the rows in view, so scrolling,
595	   120	        animations, and new output stay smooth. While the end of the output is
596	   121	        scrolled out of view, raw harness output that would only change the
597	   122	        waiting row at the end redraws nothing.
598	   123	
599	   124	    legibility:
600	   125	        The output from a realtime agent should be readable and
601	   126	        meaningful.  Make sure the font size is large enough, that the colours
602	   127	        are legible.
