=== spec/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
     3	from /ui/components/selection-popover import SelectionPopoverScope
     4	from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
     5	from /scope/project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     6	from /scope/lsp import LSP
     7	from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
     8	from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
     9	from /ui/components/history-list import HistoryListScope
    10	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
    11	
    12	export scope ChatInputScope:
    13	    concept: {ChatInputConcept}
    14	
    15	concept ChatInputConcept:
    16	    pitch:
    17	        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
    18	        as snippets of Piton.
    19	
    20	    shape: {ChatInputShape}
    21	
    22	shape ChatInputShape:
    23	    description:
    24	        Input on the left, send button on the right.
    25	
    26	        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
    27	        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}
    28	
    29	        Sending is never blocked by the harness working: while it is, the send
    30	        button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue" and sending adds
    31	        the prompt to prompt mode's queue. On the Ask tab it always reads
    32	        "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled
    33	        while the input is empty.
    34	
    35	    tabs:
    36	        overview:
    37	            The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using
    38	            gpui-kit's default tab styling. There are four tabs, in order: Code,
    39	            Chain, Spec, and Ask. Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain
    40	            is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All
    41	            four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has
    42	            more padding than a normal tab.
    43	
    44	            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
    45	            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
    46	            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
    47	
    48	            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
    49	            Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
    50	            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
    51	            not <Cmd>.
    52	
    53	            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
    54	            either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
    55	            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
    56	            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.
    57	
    58	        chain:
    59	            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
    60	            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
    61	            selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its
    62	            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
    63	            is selected.
    64	
    65	            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
    66	            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
    67	            them.
    68	
    69	            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
    70	            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
    71	            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
    72	            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
    73	            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
    74	            Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified
    75	            tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent
    76	            background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec
    77	            show through underneath it.
    78	
    79	        help:
    80	            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
    81	            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
    82	            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
    83	            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
    84	            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
    85	            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
    86	
    87	            code:
    88	                Changes the code, leaving the spec as it is.
    89	
    90	            chain:
    91	                Changes the code and the spec together.
    92	
    93	            spec:
    94	                Changes the spec, leaving the code as it is.
    95	
    96	            ask:
    97	                Asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither.
    98	
    99	        colour:
   100	            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted: a
   101	            subtle red for Code, a subtle blue for Spec, and a subtle green for
   102	            Ask. With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple.
   103	            The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes,
   104	            straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap
   105	            around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's
   106	            red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green;
   107	            neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.
   108	
   109	    systemPrompt:
   110	        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode gives
   111	        the hidden anchor a systemPrompt property alongside its userPrompt. The
   112	        code location is `codeRoot` and the spec location is `root`, as set in
   113	        the project's piton.config.pi.
   114	
   115	        defaults:
   116	            Each mode's default system prompt is the template saved for it in
   117	            this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts`
   118	            directory, one Markdown file per mode: code.md, combined.md for
   119	            Chain, spec.md, and ask.md. They are the source of truth for the
   120	            defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a
   121	            build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them
   122	            changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
   123	            without them.
   124	
   125	            The defaults are only where a project starts: each is saved with the
   126	            project and can be edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}.
   127	
   128	        A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.
   129	
   130	    ask:
   131	        Ask is for simply asking a question. A question runs straight away,
   132	        separately from any Code, Chain, or Spec task, even while the harness is
   133	        working on one. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run
   134	        at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already
   135	        running.
   136	
   137	        Each question's progress and results are shown in a task table, as in
   138	        the @{MessageList}. The questions stack directly above the tabs, the
   139	        newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make
   140	        room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is
   141	        ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an
   142	        animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While
   143	        the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest
   144	        thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and
   145	        first line.
   146	
   147	        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
   148	        and first line, above its full task table, in the answer drawer, which
   149	        it fills, scrolling once it is taller, with a @{ScrollbarScope} and its
   150	        lock to the bottom. Only one question is open at a time: opening another
   151	        closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the
   152	        stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down
   153	        to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it
   154	        again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it
   155	        if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question
   156	        becomes a previous answer.
   157	
   158	    answerSteps:
   159	        For a question, only the answer matters, so the steps leading up to it
   160	        are collapsed by default wherever a finished question's task table
   161	        is shown: an open question, and a previous answer. The steps are every
   162	        row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the
   163	        rows after it. In their place, the table's first row reads "Show 1 step"
   164	        or "Show N steps", muted, beside a right chevron, with the answer
   165	        beneath it. A single click on that row expands the steps in place, above
   166	        the answer, and the row then reads "Hide 1 step" or "Hide N steps"
   167	        beside a down chevron; clicking it again collapses them. Each question's
   168	        table is expanded or collapsed on its own, and a question closed into
   169	        the previous answers starts collapsed again.
   170	
   171	        A reply with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has
   172	        nothing to collapse and shows whole. A question still running shows its
   173	        latest step as usual. Tasks are never collapsed like this, since their
   174	        whole chain is of interest: see the @{MessageList}.
   175	
   176	    previousAnswers:
   177	        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
   178	        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
   179	        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
   180	        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
   181	        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
   182	        "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the
   183	        answer drawer, the list sliding up from on top of any question rows
   184	        still in the stack, rather than out of the chat input over them: those
   185	        rows stay where they were, in view and undimmed, beneath the drawer, and
   186	        with no rows left there it slides up out of the chat input as usual. The
   187	        questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them
   188	        left off.
   189	
   190	    answerDrawer:
   191	        Only a question open onto its task table, or the previous answers
   192	        expanded, are a drawer. Unlike the stack of question rows, which pushes
   193	        what is above it, the drawer slides up out of the chat input over
   194	        everything above it, the message list, any file beside it, and the
   195	        stack, covering them rather than pushing them, and dims them: see the
   196	        @{MessageList}. The previous answers are the exception: they slide up
   197	        from on top of the question rows in the stack, leaving those rows
   198	        uncovered and undimmed, and the drawer's share of the space counts from
   199	        the chat input, rows included. Closing it slides nothing back; the stack
   200	        and the message list are where they were beneath it.
   201	
   202	        The drawer opens to 80% of the height of the space above the chat input
   203	        by default: the open question's table, or the previous answers list,
   204	        grows to fill whatever the drawer's other rows leave, rather than
   205	        stopping at a fixed height. It slides up out of the chat input as it
   206	        opens.
   207	
   208	        While open, the drawer is resizable by dragging its top edge, which
   209	        shows a resize cursor and a thin highlight when hovered. It follows the
   210	        pointer exactly, with no slide, and can be dragged from 20% to 95% of
   211	        that space. The size it is dragged to is kept for as long as the
   212	        application runs, for every question or list opened afterwards, rather
   213	        than going back to 80%.
   214	
   215	    selectingAnswerText:
   216	        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
   217	        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
   218	        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
   219	        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
   220	        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
   221	
   222	        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
   223	        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
   224	        popover also closes when the drawer closes.
   225	
   226	    attachments:
   227	        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
   228	        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
   229	        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
   230	        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
   231	        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
   232	        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
   233	        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
   234	
   235	        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
   236	        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
   237	        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
   238	        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
   239	        the attachments it was sent with.
   240	
   241	    escape:
   242	        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
   243	        input.
   244	
   245	    growToFit:
   246	        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at
   247	        most. Its single row lines up with the send button.
   248	
   249	    autoFocus:
   250	        The chat input should be auto-focused.
   251	
   252	    syntaxHighlighting:
   253	        Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter
   254	        Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)
   255	
   256	    lsp: @{LSP}
   257	
   258	    harnessMentions:
   259	        overview:
   260	            Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@`
   261	            offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself.
   262	            The placeholder mentions both.
   263	
   264	        trigger:
   265	            A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after
   266	            whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at
   267	            sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference.
   268	            Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after
   269	            each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that
   270	            follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger;
   271	            outside of one they never reach the @{LSP}.
   272	
   273	        offered:
   274	            Skills and commands are those of the selected
   275	            ${ProjectDirectoryScope}, of the user, and of the user's enabled
   276	            plugins, a plugin's own being named `plugin:name`. Agents come from
   277	            the same places, plus the harness's built-in agents. Each shows
   278	            whether it is a skill, command, or agent, and its description as
   279	            documentation when it has one. Every harness run reports the skills
   280	            and agents it has, built-in ones included; the last report is saved
   281	            with the project and offered too. Results are narrowed and ordered
   282	            like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before
   283	            matches anywhere in it, then by name.
   284	
   285	        accepting:
   286	            Accepting a skill or command inserts `/name `, and accepting an
   287	            agent inserts `@agent-name `, which the harness understands as a
   288	            request to use that agent. They pass through the hidden anchor and
   289	            its compilation unchanged, so a prompt starting with `/name` runs
   290	            that skill or command. Mentions work without the @{LSP}.
   291	
   292	    hiddenAnchor:
   293	        While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes,
   294	        they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt
   295	        property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the
   296	        @{HarnessIntegrationScope}
   297	
   298	        escaping:
   299	            A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it
   300	            isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, quotes,
   301	            colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and
   302	            backslashes all mean something. Its userPrompt is a list with an
   303	            item per line of the prompt, in order, and each line a list of its
   304	            pieces: the text between references as a quoted string, with
   305	            quotes, backslashes, and each dollar-brace escaped, so nothing in it
   306	            is interpolated or evaluated; and each at-brace or dollar-brace
   307	            around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported as
   308	            a reference of its own. A reference to a name that isn't imported,
   309	            such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. An empty line is a
   310	            single empty string. The compiled userPrompt is the pieces of each
   311	            line joined together, and the lines joined by line breaks, so what
   312	            the harness receives is exactly what was typed or pasted, line for
   313	            line, with each reference resolved. The systemPrompt is written the
   314	            same way. A prompt saved as prose by an earlier version still reads
   315	            back.
   316	
   317	        autoImports:
   318	            The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there,
   319	            typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the
   320	            prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position
   321	            for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other
   322	            than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out,
   323	            character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or
   324	            brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment
   325	            then never stops the server finding the names that need importing,
   326	            both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.
   327	
   328	        attachedText:
   329	            A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText
   330	            property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the
   331	            order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not
   332	            as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a
   333	            quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it
   334	            is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no
   335	            attachedText property.
   336	
   337	            What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the
   338	            attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a
   339	            fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks
   340	            in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the
   341	            task's header.
=== spec/scope/prompt-mode/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from ./chat-input import ChatInputScope
     3	from ./message-list import MessageList
     4	from /ui/components/history-list import HistoryListScope
     5	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
     6	from /ui/components/git-panel import GitPanelScope
     7	
     8	export scope PromptEditor:
     9	    concept: {PromptEditorConcept}
    10	
    11	concept PromptEditorConcept:
    12	    pitch:
    13	        An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude
    14	        Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.
    15	
    16	    shape: {PromptEditorShape}
    17	
    18	shape PromptEditorShape:
    19	    description:
    20	        Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can
    21	        queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no
    22	        message bubbles.
    23	
    24	    basicDesignAndLayout:
    25	        The @{MessageList} fills all available space except for a
    26	        @{ChatInputScope} along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the
    27	        previous tasks row, the header for the latest task, the latest task's
    28	        output, and the queue.
    29	
    30	        Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which
    31	        wraps when the view is narrow. It reads
    32	        "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it."
    33	        or, while no project is open, "Open a project to start prompting."
    34	
    35	    chatHistory: @{MessageList}
    36	
    37	    previousTasks:
    38	        Previous tasks are a @{HistoryListScope} along the top of the view,
    39	        listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but the latest,
    40	        which heads the view: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or
    41	        "N previous tasks". Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest
    42	        task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".
    43	
    44	    header:
    45	        The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working:
    46	        its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the
    47	        hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the
    48	        harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it
    49	        has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead.
    50	
    51	    queue:
    52	        overview:
    53	            Prompts can still be sent while the harness is working: they wait
    54	            in a queue, in the order they were sent, and are sent one at a
    55	            time. While the harness is working, the chat input's send button
    56	            reads "Queue".
    57	
    58	            A question from the Ask tab never queues. It runs straight away,
    59	            even while the harness is working on a task.
    60	
    61	        placement:
    62	            The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and
    63	            directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is
    64	            not part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued,
    65	            with a chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line
    66	            or two of each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list
    67	            is numbered, with its number, text, and cancel button vertically
    68	            centred in its row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a
    69	            @{ScrollbarScope}. Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to
    70	            the bottom, on the prompts queued most recently, however it was
    71	            scrolled when last closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch
    72	            and the "Send next" button.
    73	            The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.
    74	
    75	        cancel:
    76	            A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which
    77	            removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no
    78	            longer in the queue.
    79	
    80	        autoSend:
    81	            A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending the next
    82	            queued prompt as soon as the harness is free, and waiting. It starts
    83	            switched on. Switching it on while the harness is free sends the
    84	            next queued prompt straight away. Whenever the harness is free and
    85	            the queue is not empty, a "Send next" button sends the first queued
    86	            prompt. A prompt that fails to compile or run does not stop the
    87	            queue.
    88	
    89	        persistence:
    90	            Queued prompts are saved in the project's `.suspense/queue`
    91	            directory, each as its hidden anchor's source, imports included,
    92	            the way prompt history is, and named so they list in the order they
    93	            were queued. The queue is restored whenever the project is opened;
    94	            a restored queue waits for "Send next" rather than sending on its
    95	            own. A queued prompt's file is removed when it is cancelled, or
    96	            when it is sent, at which point it is saved to the prompt history
    97	            like any other prompt.
    98	
    99	    buildingTheSpec:
   100	        Before a Code, Chain, or Spec prompt is sent, `piton build` runs in the
   101	        project, so the compiled spec the harness reads is up to date. It runs
   102	        when the prompt is actually sent, so a queued prompt builds when its
   103	        turn comes, not when it is queued. The task shows "Building" until the
   104	        build is over. A build that fails does not stop the prompt, since the
   105	        prompt may be the one to fix the spec: the task's output starts with
   106	        an error saying the build failed, so the compiled spec may be out of
   107	        date, with what the build reported. A question from the Ask tab is sent
   108	        without building.
   109	
   110	    commitNote:
   111	        Once a Code, Chain, or Spec task finishes without error, it adds a
   112	        commit note summarising what it changed to the @{GitPanelScope}.
   113	
   114	    history:
   115	        Every task sent is saved in the project's `.suspense/history` directory
   116	        as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the
   117	        anchor's name. Once its run is over, what came of it is saved beside it
   118	        in a `.json` file of the same name: the compiled userPrompt the harness
   119	        received, each line the harness printed, and any error. Opening the
   120	        project brings back every task in order, with its output replayed from
   121	        that record. A task with no record shows as "Not recorded".
   122	
   123	        Every question asked from the Ask tab is logged the same way, but in
   124	        the project's `.suspense/asks` directory instead, so it never comes back
   125	        as a task: its hidden anchor's source, and beside it a `.json` record
   126	        of what came of it. The record is saved when the run is over, and also
   127	        when the question is closed or replaced while it runs, with as much as
   128	        the harness had done. A question that fails before it reaches the
   129	        harness is logged too, with the error in its record.
   130	
   131	    chatInput: @{ChatInputScope}

     1	use /lib
     2	from /scope/editor import EditorScope
     3	from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
     4	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
     5	
     6	export scope MessageList:
     7	    concept: {MessageListConcept}
     8	
     9	concept MessageListConcept:
    10	    pitch:
    11	        The task view of prompt mode: the tasks sent to the harness and their
    12	        output as the harness works on them.
    13	
    14	    shape: {MessageListShape}
    15	
    16	shape MessageListShape:
    17	    description:
    18	        Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown
    19	        on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered
    20	        into groups.
    21	
    22	    sentPrompt:
    23	        A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to
    24	        the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the
    25	        name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.
    26	
    27	    status:
    28	        A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in
    29	        blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green,
    30	        "Failed" in red, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history
    31	        with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and
    32	        dark mode.
    33	
    34	    outputTable:
    35	        A task's output is a table with Type, Output, and Status columns, with
    36	        one row per thing the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text,
    37	        each tool call, and any error.
    38	
    39	        Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply" and errors
    40	        are "Error". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and
    41	        NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit;
    42	        "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for
    43	        WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for
    44	        anything else.
    45	
    46	        A tool call's status is "running", "done", or "failed", and a call still
    47	        running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in.
    48	
    49	        Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What
    50	        subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a
    51	        final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished task with
    52	        nothing to show reads "No output."
    53	
    54	    toolCalls:
    55	        A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files,
    56	        Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since
    57	        the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first.
    58	
    59	        Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the
    60	        project directory itself reads `.`.
    61	
    62	        A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long
    63	        one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per
    64	        line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes,
    65	        command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs. Other arguments
    66	        are shown on a single line.
    67	
    68	    running:
    69	        While a task is under way, its table ends in a row for whatever the
    70	        harness does next. Until a row has something meaningful to show, its
    71	        Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last three lines
    72	        of the harness's raw output: muted, monospace, JSON syntax-highlighted,
    73	        and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump. Before any output
    74	        has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…". As soon as a row's type
    75	        is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its text or argument
    76	        arrives, that is shown. While the input of a Files, Edit, Command, Web,
    77	        or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell shows only a skeleton.
    78	
    79	    runningSkeleton:
    80	        A skeleton stands in for a currently running task only while there is
    81	        nothing meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is anything
    82	        meaningful to display for that task in the message list, no skeleton is
    83	        shown for it at all.
    84	
    85	    links:
    86	        Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to
    87	        a file opens it in the @{EditorScope} beside the task view, a web link
    88	        opens in the browser, and a link to a file that doesn't exist shows an
    89	        error notification. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit
    90	        row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.
    91	
    92	    backgrounds:
    93	        The header for the latest task is coloured like the tab the task was
    94	        sent from, the same colour the @{ChatInputScope} body shows for that
    95	        tab: a subtle red for Code, purple for Chain, and a subtle blue for
    96	        Spec. A task from the history that doesn't say which tab it was sent
    97	        from keeps the tab bar's colour. The queue along the bottom and the
    98	        previous tasks row along the top both have the same background colour as
    99	        the tab bar.
   100	
   101	    askDimming:
   102	        While a finished question from the Ask tab is open onto its full task
   103	        table, a dark shade fades in over the message list to draw attention to
   104	        it, and fades back out when it is closed or closed down to its row. The
   105	        shade also shows while the previous answers are expanded on the Ask
   106	        tab: while the answer drawer is open. Question rows in the stack above
   107	        the tabs, running or finished, never dim the list; they push it up
   108	        instead. The shade covers all the space above the chat input beneath the
   109	        drawer: the message list, any file open beside it, and the stack of
   110	        question rows.
   111	
   112	    scrolling:
   113	        The latest task's output scrolls with a @{ScrollbarScope}, with its
   114	        lock to the bottom. Unlocked, it still follows new output while it is
   115	        already scrolled to the bottom. The lock is off until switched on.
   116	
   117	        The rows of the output table scroll beneath its header, which stays at
   118	        the top. However long the output or the list of previous tasks grows,
   119	        drawing it costs no more than drawing the rows in view, so scrolling,
   120	        animations, and new output stay smooth. While the end of the output is
   121	        scrolled out of view, raw harness output that would only change the
   122	        waiting row at the end redraws nothing.
   123	
   124	    legibility:
   125	        The output from a realtime agent should be readable and
   126	        meaningful.  Make sure the font size is large enough, that the colours
   127	        are legible.

=== spec/ui/components/ribbon/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /ui/components/project-indicator import ProjectIndicator
     3	from ./project-tab import RibbonProjectTabScope
     4	from ./code-tab import RibbonCodeTabScope
     5	from ./spec-tab import RibbonSpecTabScope
     6	from ./research-tab import RibbonResearchTabScope
     7	from ./application-tab import RibbonApplicationTabScope
     8	
     9	export scope RibbonScope:
    10	    concept: {RibbonConcept}
    11	
    12	concept RibbonConcept:
    13	    pitch:
    14	        The ribbon along the top of the main window: tabs, each holding the
    15	        application's commands for one area of work in labelled groups.
    16	
    17	    shape: {RibbonShape}
    18	
    19	shape RibbonShape:
    20	    description:
    21	        A ribbon runs along the top of the window, using gpui-kit's Tab
    22	        component with its default styling. Its tabs are, in order: Project,
    23	        Code, Spec, Research, and Application. The window always opens on
    24	        Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups.
    25	        There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.
    26	
    27	    openingSeveralTabs:
    28	        Clicking a tab opens it alone, as usual. Ctrl+clicking one (Cmd+click on
    29	        macOS) opens it alongside whichever tabs are already open, or, if it is
    30	        already open, closes it, so any number of tabs can be open at once. The
    31	        last open tab can't be closed this way: Ctrl+clicking it leaves it open.
    32	        Every open tab shows as selected.
    33	
    34	        The command area then holds the groups of every open tab side by side,
    35	        in the order of the tabs rather than the order they were opened, with no
    36	        divider between one tab's groups and the next, as between any groups. An
    37	        open tab with no commands adds nothing, and "No commands yet" shows only
    38	        when none of the open tabs has any. When the groups are wider than the
    39	        window, the command area scrolls sideways. The command area stays the
    40	        same height however many tabs are open.
    41	
    42	        Double-clicking a tab still collapses the ribbon, and expanding it again
    43	        shows the same tabs open. Which tabs are open isn't kept between
    44	        launches: the window always opens with only Project open.
    45	
    46	    activity:
    47	        While anything is running, a small spinner sits just to the right of the
    48	        project indicator, as it is beside the tabs or leading the collapsed
    49	        ribbon, with how many things are running beside it when more than one
    50	        is. Its tooltip says what is running, or how many things are. While
    51	        nothing is, neither shows, and nothing takes their place.
    52	
    53	        Clicking the spinner opens a small list beneath it of everything
    54	        running, one row each, the newest last: the task the harness is working
    55	        on, headed "Task" with the first line of its prompt; each question still
    56	        running, headed "Question" with its first line; a spec build,
    57	        "Building the spec"; a divergence analysis, "Analyzing divergence"; and
    58	        a search for concepts to rescope, "Finding scopes to extract".
    59	        Each row has a small spinner of its own. Clicking a row closes the list
    60	        and reveals what it is: a task brings back the latest task's output,
    61	        closing the previous tasks and any inset panel over it, and scrolls it
    62	        to the end; a question closes the answer drawer and any inset panel, so
    63	        its row is in view; a divergence analysis or a rescope search brings its
    64	        panel back. A spec
    65	        build has nothing to show, so its row only closes the list. Pressing the
    66	        mouse outside the list, or <Escape>, closes it too, as does everything
    67	        in it finishing.
    68	
    69	    projectIndicator:
    70	        To the left of the tabs, in the same bar, sits the @{ProjectIndicator},
    71	        with a thin vertical divider between it and the first tab.
    72	
    73	    groups:
    74	        Each group has its title in muted text rotated -90deg (bottom to top)
    75	        aligned along the left edge of the group naming what its commands have
    76	        in common. The title sits on a strip with a slightly different
    77	        background colour, at 12px, with generous padding either side of it
    78	        within the strip. Groups sit side by side with no divider between
    79	        them: each group's title strip is what marks where it starts.
    80	
    81	        A tab with no commands reads "No commands yet".
    82	
    83	    tabs:
    84	        Each tab is a scope of its own, which says what groups and commands it
    85	        holds, and what each command does.
    86	
    87	        project: @{RibbonProjectTabScope}
    88	
    89	        code: @{RibbonCodeTabScope}
    90	
    91	        spec: @{RibbonSpecTabScope}
    92	
    93	        research: @{RibbonResearchTabScope}
    94	
    95	        application: @{RibbonApplicationTabScope}
    96	
    97	    commands:
    98	        A command button shows a large icon above its label. An on or off
    99	        setting, like dark mode, is a switch rather than a button.
   100	
   101	        A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its
   102	        label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
   103	
   104	        A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands
   105	        are.
   106	
   107	        A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says
   108	        why.
   109	
   110	    height:
   111	        The command area is the same height on every tab, even one with no
   112	        commands, so the window beneath doesn't move when switching tabs.
   113	
   114	    collapsing:
   115	        The ribbon collapses, and expands again, with a chevron button at the
   116	        right end of the ribbon, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1
   117	        (Cmd+F1 on macOS). Whether it is collapsed is saved for the user and
   118	        restored on the next launch.
   119	
   120	        Collapsed, the tabs go away too. The ribbon becomes a single thin row
   121	        led by the project indicator, as it is beside the tabs and with the same
   122	        divider after it, and then holding every primary command, from all of
   123	        the tabs, as small buttons: a small icon beside its label, and dark mode
   124	        as a small switch. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin
   125	        vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep
   126	        their tooltips and disabled states. The chevron sits at the right end of
   127	        the row. Every control in the row, the chevron and the dividers
   128	        included, is vertically centred in it.
=== spec/ui/components/ribbon/spec-tab/index.pi
     1	use /lib

    13	    shape: {RibbonSpecTabShape}
    14	
    15	shape RibbonSpecTabShape:
    16	    description:
    17	        The Spec tab of the ribbon.
    18

    21	            A "Build" group holds the Build Spec command.
    22	
    23	        analysis:
    24	            An "Analysis" group, after Build, holds the Analyze Divergence
    25	            command, then the View Divergence Reports command.
    26	
    27	        skills:
    28	            A "Skills" group, after Analysis, holds the Generate Skills command.

    69	
    70	            It isn't primary.
    71

    80	
    81	            When the build is over, a notification says how it went. A build

=== spec/ui/components/git-panel/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
     3	from /ui/components/file-tree import FileTreeScope
     4	from /scope/project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
     5	from /scope/git import GitScope
     6	
     7	export scope GitPanelScope:
     8	    concept: {GitPanelConcept}
     9	
    10	concept GitPanelConcept:
    11	    pitch:
    12	        A very basic git panel for the repository the
    13	        ${ProjectDirectoryScope} is in, as the @{GitScope} knows it: see what
    14	        has changed at a glance, write a commit message, commit, push, and
    15	        pull.
    16	
    17	    shape: {GitPanelShape}
    18	
    19	shape GitPanelShape:
    20	    description:
    21	        A compact panel with a thin border along its top. It is shown only
    22	        while the project is inside a git repository.
    23	
    24	    branch:
    25	        The top row shows the branch from the @{GitScope}, or
    26	        "Detached HEAD", beside how many commits it is ahead of its upstream
    27	        (↑) and behind it (↓), each only when not zero. At the right end are a Pull button and a Push
    28	        button, icons with tooltips.
    29	
    30	    summary:
    31	        Below the branch, a line counts the @{GitScope}'s changes, leaving out
    32	        any kind with none, as "2 modified · 1 untracked", or "No changes".
    33	        Beside it, how many lines were added (+, in green) and removed (−, in
    34	        red). The files themselves are not listed, since the @{FileTreeScope}
    35	        shows them. The summary refreshes as the @{GitScope} does, and
    36	        straight after anything the panel does.
    37	
    38	    commitNotes:
    39	        Above the message box, a row for each commit note, in the order they
    40	        were added: a one-line box holding the note, which can be edited, and a
    41	        small button to remove it. Each Code, Chain, or Spec task that finishes
    42	        without error adds a note, a one-line summary of what the task changed,
    43	        once the harness has written it, quickly, in the same way as a written
    44	        message: from what the task asked and the harness's own summary of what
    45	        it did, at most 72 characters in the imperative mood, as
    46	        system-prompts/commit-note.pi asks. A task that
    47	        changed no files adds none, and neither does a question from the Ask
    48	        tab. Notes are saved with the project, in its
    49	        `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, as they are added, edited, and removed,
    50	        so they survive a restart; that file is never itself committed.
    51	
    52	    message:
    53	        A commit message box, a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 10 rows at
    54	        most, so it starts at a single row. It reads "Commit message" while
    55	        empty.
    56	
    57	    writingAMessage:
    58	        A "Write message" button, with a sparkles icon, has the harness write
    59	        the commit message from what has changed, and puts it in the message
    60	        box, replacing what was there. It is quick: a small, fast model, at
    61	        low effort, with no tools, handed only the list of changed files and
    62	        as much of the diff as fits in a small, fixed amount. The message is a
    63	        summary line of at most 72 characters in the imperative mood,
    64	        followed, only if it helps, by a few short bullet points, as
    65	        system-prompts/commit-message.pi asks. The button
    66	        is disabled while there are no changes.
    67	
    68	    committing:
    69	        A primary "Commit" button commits every change, new files included.
    70	        The commit message is what was typed, then a blank line, then each
    71	        note that isn't blank as a line of its own starting "- "; with nothing
    72	        typed, it is the notes alone. Once committed, the message box and the
    73	        notes are cleared. It is disabled while there is neither a message nor
    74	        a note, or there are no changes.
    75	
    76	    pushingAndPulling:
    77	        Push pushes the branch, setting its upstream on origin first if it has
    78	        none.
    79	
    80	        Pull fetches the branch's upstream. With nothing new it says the
    81	        branch is already up to date. When only the upstream has moved on, the
    82	        branch fast-forwards to it. When both have moved on, the upstream is
    83	        merged in automatically, as long as the merge has no conflicts. If it
    84	        would conflict, the pull is cancelled before anything changes: the
    85	        branch, its files, and the index stay exactly as they were, no merge is
    86	        left in progress, and an error names the files that would have
    87	        conflicted. Pull is disabled while the branch has no upstream.
    88	
    89	    feedback:
    90	        While the panel is committing, pushing, pulling, or writing a
    91	        message, that button shows a spinner and the others are disabled.
    92	        Committing, pushing, and pulling say so in a notification when they
    93	        succeed; a pull says whether it was already up to date, pulled, or
    94	        pulled and merged. Anything that fails says why in an error notification.
=== spec/ui/components/history-list/index.pi

    10	        A way back to everything sent before of one kind, such as previous tasks
    11	        or previous answers: a small row that expands into a list of every one
    12	        of them.
    13	
    14	    shape: {HistoryListShape}
    15	
    16	shape HistoryListShape:
    17	    description:
    18	        The same row and list, looking and behaving the same, wherever something
    19	        sent before can be looked back on. Each use names what it lists, what
    20	        the row counts, and what the row reads while expanded.
    21	
    22	    row:
    23	        A small row, always shown where it is used, with the tab bar's
    24	        background colour. It reads "No …", "1 …", or "N …" followed by what it
    25	        counts, beside a chevron, and does nothing until there is anything to
    26	        list. Clicking it expands the list, and the row then reads what it says
    27	        to go back; clicking it again closes the list.
    28	
    29	    list:
    30	        A scrollable accordion of every item, oldest first, with a
    31	        @{ScrollbarScope}. Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the
    32	        bottom, with the most recent items in view, however it was scrolled

    34	        takes the place of the latest task or slides up as a drawer. Each is headed by its
    35	        status and the first line of its prompt, and opens onto the compiled
    36	        prompt it was sent as and its task table, as in the @{MessageList}. One
    37	        item is open at a time. A use can say its tables collapse the steps
    38	        leading up to the result, as previous answers do; previous tasks show
    39	        their tables whole.

    42	        in its prompt or table, which wrap rather than running past the
    43	        list's edge, and exactly as tall as what it shows: it ends a small
    44	        margin below its table, like the margin above its prompt, with no
    45	        empty space beneath it before the next item or the end of the list.
=== spec/ui/components/diff-view/index.pi
     1	use /lib
     2	from /scope/git import GitScope
     3	from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
     4	
     5	export scope DiffViewScope:
     6	    concept: {DiffViewConcept}
     7	
     8	concept DiffViewConcept:
     9	    pitch:
    10	        A view of one file's uncommitted changes: the file as of the last
    11	        commit, from the @{GitScope}, against the file as it is on disk.
    12	
    13	    shape: {DiffViewShape}
    14

use /lib
from /ui/animations/rise-in import RiseInAnimation

export scope InsetPanelScope:
    concept: {InsetPanelConcept}

concept InsetPanelConcept:
    pitch:
        A floating panel over the whole main window, for work that needs more
        room than a popup and shouldn't disturb what is beneath it.

    shape: {InsetPanelShape}

shape InsetPanelShape:
    description:
        The panel floats over everything in the window, the ribbon and sidebar
        included, inset 32 pixels from every edge of the window. It has rounded
        corners, a border, and a shadow, and whatever it holds fills it. The
        window behind it is dimmed, and nothing behind it takes the mouse while
        it is open. Only one panel is open at a time.

    animating:
        The panel comes in each time it opens and goes away each time it closes
        with the @{RiseInAnimation}: the panel is its surface, and the dimmed
        window around the panel is its dimming. Switching what the panel holds,
        such as opening a diff while the settings are open, swaps it in place.

    modal:
        While the panel is open, nothing beneath it can take focus or input;
        only the panel and what it holds can.

        The mouse can't reach anything beneath: no clicks, scrolling, hovering,
        or tooltips, except that clicking the dimmed window closes the panel.

        Focus moves into the panel when it opens and can't leave it. <Tab> and
        <Shift+Tab> cycle through what can be focused within the panel, going
        round from the last back to the first and the other way, rather than on
        to anything beneath. Anything that would move focus beneath while it is
        open, such as a task beneath finishing, sends focus back into the panel
        instead.

        The main window's shortcuts that act on what is beneath do nothing while
        it is open: opening the palette with <Ctrl+P> (<Cmd+P> on macOS), and
        collapsing or expanding the ribbon with <Ctrl+F1> (<Cmd+F1> on macOS).
        Shortcuts that open something of their own, like the settings window, or
        quitting, still work.

    closing:
        The panel closes with a close or cancel button in what it holds, with
        <Escape>, or by clicking the dimmed window around it; clicking inside
        the panel never closes it. Once it closes, focus goes back to the chat
        input.

use /lib
from /ui/animations/rise-in import RiseInAnimation

export scope InsetPanelScope:
    concept: {InsetPanelConcept}

concept InsetPanelConcept:
    pitch:
        A floating panel over the whole main window, for work that needs more
        room than a popup and shouldn't disturb what is beneath it.

    shape: {InsetPanelShape}

shape InsetPanelShape:
    description:
        The panel floats over everything in the window, the ribbon and sidebar
        included, inset 32 pixels from every edge of the window. It has rounded
        corners, a border, and a shadow, and whatever it holds fills it. The
        window behind it is dimmed, and nothing behind it takes the mouse while
        it is open. Only one panel is open at a time.

    animating:
        The panel comes in each time it opens and goes away each time it closes
        with the @{RiseInAnimation}: the panel is its surface, and the dimmed
        window around the panel is its dimming. Switching what the panel holds,
        such as opening a diff while the settings are open, swaps it in place.

    modal:
        While the panel is open, nothing beneath it can take focus or input;
        only the panel and what it holds can.

        The mouse can't reach anything beneath: no clicks, scrolling, hovering,
        or tooltips, except that clicking the dimmed window closes the panel.

        Focus moves into the panel when it opens and can't leave it. <Tab> and
        <Shift+Tab> cycle through what can be focused within the panel, going
        round from the last back to the first and the other way, rather than on
        to anything beneath. Anything that would move focus beneath while it is
        open, such as a task beneath finishing, sends focus back into the panel
        instead.

        The main window's shortcuts that act on what is beneath do nothing while
        it is open: opening the palette with <Ctrl+P> (<Cmd+P> on macOS), and
        collapsing or expanding the ribbon with <Ctrl+F1> (<Cmd+F1> on macOS).
        Shortcuts that open something of their own, like the settings window, or
        quitting, still work.

    closing:
        The panel closes with a close or cancel button in what it holds, with
        <Escape>, or by clicking the dimmed window around it; clicking inside
        the panel never closes it. Once it closes, focus goes back to the chat
        input.

use /lib
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export scope TaskTableScope:
    concept: {TaskTableConcept}

concept TaskTableConcept:
    pitch:
        The output of one run of the harness, as a table of everything it did,
        filling in as it does it.

    shape: {TaskTableShape}

shape TaskTableShape:
    description:
        A table with Type, Output, and Status columns, with one row per thing
        the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text, each tool call, and
        any error. It is the same table wherever a run's output is shown, a
        task, a question, a previous task or answer, the palette's search for a
        file, or a run in one of the application's own panels, and each use
        says where it sits.

    types:
        Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply" and errors
        are "Error". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and
        NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit;
        "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for
        WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for
        anything else.

    status:
        A tool call's status is "running", "done", or "failed", and a call still
        running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in.

    replies:
        Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What
        subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a
        final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished run with
        nothing to show reads "No output."

    toolCalls:
        A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files,
        Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since
        the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first.

        Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the
        project directory itself reads `.`.

        A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long
        one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per
        line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes,
        command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs. Other arguments
        are shown on a single line.

    streaming:
        While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for
        whatever the harness does next. Until a row has something meaningful to
        show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last
        three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON
        syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump.
        Before any output has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…". As
        soon as a row's type is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its
        text or argument arrives, that is shown. While the input of a Files,
        Edit, Command, Web, or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell
        shows only a skeleton.

        A skeleton stands in for a running row only while there is nothing
        meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is, no skeleton is shown for
        it at all.

    scrolling:
        The rows scroll beneath the table's header, which stays at the top,
        with a @{ScrollbarScope} and its lock to the bottom. Locked, the table
        follows the run's latest output. Unlocked, it still follows new output
        while it is already scrolled to the bottom, and stays put once scrolled
        away from it. Each use says whether the lock starts on.

        However long the output grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing
        the rows in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.
        While the end of the table is scrolled out of view, raw output that
        would only change the waiting row redraws nothing.

    collapsedSteps:
        A use can say its table collapses the steps leading up to the answer,
        once the run is finished. The steps are every row up to and including
        the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it. In their
        place, the table's first row reads "Show 1 step" or "Show N steps",
        muted, beside a right chevron, with the answer beneath it. A single
        click on that row expands the steps in place, above the answer, and the
        row then reads "Hide 1 step" or "Hide N steps" beside a down chevron;
        clicking it again collapses them. Each table is expanded or collapsed on
        its own.

        A run with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has
        nothing to collapse and shows whole. A run still under way shows its
        latest step as usual.

    legibility:
        The output from a realtime agent should be readable and meaningful.
        Make sure the font size is large enough, and that the colours are
        legible in both light and dark mode.

export scope BakedSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {BakedSystemPromptsConcept}

concept BakedSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The prompts the application gives the harness for its own work, rather
        than a prompt someone writes, written in Piton and built into the
        application.

    shape: {BakedSystemPromptsShape}

shape BakedSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        The prompts are Piton files in the repository's system-prompts folder,
        one for each piece of the application's own work:
        - divergence.pi, for the two agents of a divergence analysis
        - generate-skills.pi, for ranking the spec's scopes for skills
        - rescope.pi, for finding concepts to extract into scopes, and for the refactoring prompt sent for those chosen
        - commit-note.pi, for a finished task's commit note
        - commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
        - file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description

    writing:
        Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for
        each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a
        heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a name
        in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.

    building:
        They are compiled with `piton compile` when the application is built,
        and built into it: changing one changes what the next build sends, and
        a prompt that doesn't compile fails the build, with piton's error. Each
        build keeps what it compiled in system-prompts/compiled.json, with the
        source, so the application still builds where `piton` isn't installed,
        such as on CI, from the prompts as last compiled, saying so.

    modePrompts:
        The system prompts each chat mode sends are not among them: see the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope}.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/harness-integration/baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export scope OneOffAgentRunScope:
    concept: {OneOffAgentRunConcept}

concept OneOffAgentRunConcept:
    pitch:
        A run of the harness for the application's own work, such as analyzing
        or ranking the spec, that can look at the project but never change it.

    shape: {OneOffAgentRunShape}

shape OneOffAgentRunShape:
    description:
        A separate run of the @{HarnessIntegrationScope}'s harness in the
        project directory. It keeps no session: it never carries on a
        conversation, not even one of its own, and nothing carries on from it,
        so the tasks and questions never see it. It can only read, glob, and
        search files, never change anything.

    prompt:
        Its prompt is one of the @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, with what the
        application fills in, then whatever the use hands it after, such as a
        list of files, given to the harness on its standard input.

    streaming:
        It streams its output as JSON, a line per event, text as it is written,
        shown as it arrives in a @{TaskTableScope}, whose lock to the bottom
        starts on, so it follows the run's latest output. Its reply is the
        result it finishes with.

    reply:
        It replies with nothing but JSON, shaped as its prompt asks, which each
        use describes.

    failing:
        When the harness can't be run, fails, or replies with something that
        can't be read as that JSON, the run fails, with why. Each use says what
        it does then.

    stopping:
        Closing whatever started it stops it.

use /lib
from /ui/components/inset-panel import InsetPanelScope
from /scope/running-activity import RunningActivityScope

export scope MinimizablePanelScope:
    concept: {MinimizablePanelConcept}

concept MinimizablePanelConcept:
    pitch:
        An inset panel for long-running work that can be put out of the way
        while the work carries on, and brought back to see how it went.

    shape: {MinimizablePanelShape}

shape MinimizablePanelShape:
    description:
        An @{InsetPanelScope} with a minimize button beside the close button in
        its header. Each use names its work, the command that opens it, and how
        its work is listed among the @{RunningActivityScope}.

    minimizing:
        The minimize button, whose tooltip says the work keeps running, hides
        the panel without stopping anything: the work carries on out of sight,
        and the window beneath can be used again, as when an inset panel
        closes.

        Opening another inset panel, such as a file's diff, while it is showing
        minimizes it rather than closing it. Several panels can be minimized at
        once.

    comingBack:
        A minimized panel comes back just as it was left, steps or results.
        While its work runs, its row among the @{RunningActivityScope} brings it
        back. At any time, its command brings back the minimized panel rather
        than opening another; each use says whether its command also starts its
        work again.

    closing:
        Only closing the panel, with its close button, the dimmed window around
        it, or <Escape>, stops its work, and forgets it: its command then opens
        a fresh panel.

use /lib
from /scope/no-project import NoProjectStateScope
from /scope/running-activity import RunningActivityScope

export scope SpecBuildScope:
    concept: {SpecBuildConcept}

concept SpecBuildConcept:
    pitch:
        Brings the project's compiled spec up to date, so what the harness
        reads of the spec is what the spec says now.

    shape: {SpecBuildShape}

shape SpecBuildShape:
    description:
        `piton build` runs in the project directory, compiling the spec and
        writing it out for the agents, the reference folder the harness reads
        included. A build runs either on its own, from a command, or ahead of
        other work that relies on the compiled spec.

    onItsOwn:
        The Build Spec command, and Build in the palette, run a build on their
        own. They are unavailable while no project is open, as the
        @{NoProjectStateScope} says, and while such a build is running, when the
        command shows a spinner and its tooltip says the spec is building. The
        build is listed among the @{RunningActivityScope} as
        "Building the spec".

        When the build is over, a notification says how it went. A build that
        succeeds is titled "Built 1 file" or "Built N files", and lists each
        file written on a line of its own, never wrapped. A build that fails is
        titled "Build failed", with what the build reported. When
        `piton build` can't be run at all, the notification is titled
        "Could not run piton build", with why.

    aheadOfWork:
        A build ahead of other work runs when that work actually starts, not
        when it is asked for, and shows as a step of that work until it is
        over. It isn't listed among the running activity on its own, since the
        work it leads is.

        A build that fails, or can't be run, never stops the work that follows,
        since that work may be what fixes the spec, or can go on with the
        compiled spec as it was. The work says the build failed, so the compiled
        spec may be out of date, with what the build reported.

use /lib
from /scope/prompt-mode import PromptEditor
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope
from /scope/divergence import DivergenceScope
from /scope/rescope import RescopeScope
from /ui/components/minimizable-panel import MinimizablePanelScope

export scope RunningActivityScope:
    concept: {RunningActivityConcept}

concept RunningActivityConcept:
    pitch:
        What the application is still working on, where to see it and get back
        to it, and what makes quitting ask first.

    shape: {RunningActivityShape}

shape RunningActivityShape:
    description:
        The work still running in the application, each with how it is listed,
        newest last:
        - the task the harness is working on, from the @{PromptEditor}, headed "Task" with the first line of its prompt
        - each question still running, from the @{ChatInputScope}'s Ask tab, headed "Question" with its first line
        - a spec build run on its own, as the @{SpecBuildScope} says, "Building the spec"
        - a divergence analysis in the @{DivergenceScope}, "Analyzing divergence"
        - a search for concepts to rescope in the @{RescopeScope}, "Finding scopes to extract"

        Prompts waiting in the queue don't count as running, since they are
        saved with the project, and neither does a panel whose work is over.

    indicator:
        While anything is running, a small spinner shows, with how many things
        are running beside it when more than one is. Its tooltip says what is
        running, or how many things are. While nothing is, neither shows, and
        nothing takes their place. Where it sits is up to what holds it.

    list:
        Clicking the spinner opens a small list beneath it of everything
        running, one row each, in the order above, each with a small spinner of
        its own. Clicking a row closes the list and reveals what it is:
        - a task brings back the latest task's output, closing the previous tasks and any inset panel over it, and scrolls it to the end
        - a question closes the answer drawer and any inset panel, so its row is in view
        - a divergence analysis or a rescope search brings its @{MinimizablePanelScope} back
        - a spec build has nothing to show, so its row only closes the list

        Pressing the mouse outside the list, or <Escape>, closes it too, as
        does everything in it finishing.

    quitting:
        Quitting, however it is asked for, while the harness is working on a
        task or a question, or while a spec build runs on its own, asks first.
        A divergence analysis or a rescope search doesn't ask, and quitting
        stops it. The message is titled "Quit while a task is running?" and
        says what is still running: the harness working on a prompt, piton
        build, or both. "Quit" exits, and "Keep Running" or <Escape> dismisses
        it. Asking to quit again while it is open doesn't open a second one,
        and an open palette closes first.

use /lib
from /scope/project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope

export scope ProjectDataScope:
    concept: {ProjectDataConcept}

concept ProjectDataConcept:
    pitch:
        What the application keeps for a project, kept in the project itself
        so it survives a restart and travels with the project.

    shape: {ProjectDataShape}

shape ProjectDataShape:
    description:
        Everything the application keeps for a project lives in a `.suspense`
        directory inside the @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, created as it is needed.
        Nothing about a project is kept anywhere else, apart from the draft.

    contents:
        - `history/`: every task sent, as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the anchor's name, and beside it, once its run is over, a `.json` record of the same name holding the compiled userPrompt the harness received, each line the harness printed, and any error
        - `asks/`: every question asked from the Ask tab, saved the same way as a task but apart from them
        - `queue/`: each queued prompt, as its hidden anchor's source, imports included, named so they list in the order they were queued
        - `divergence/`: each divergence report, a JSON file named by when it was made
        - `system-prompts/`: each mode's system prompt template, a Markdown file named after its mode, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md
        - `commit-notes.json`: the Git panel's commit notes
        - `harness.json`: the last report the harness gave of the skills and agents it has

        The draft, `.suspense-draft.pi`, sits in the spec location, as the
        @{ProjectLocationsScope} says, rather than in `.suspense`: it is the
        prompt being written, as `piton lsp` is shown it.

    machineOnly:
        Some of it belongs to one machine rather than to the project: the
        harness report `.suspense/harness.json`, the queue `.suspense/queue/`,
        the commit notes `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, and the draft
        `.suspense-draft.pi` wherever it is. Git ignores these, so they are
        never committed. Everything else, the prompt history, the questions,
        the divergence reports, and the system prompts, is kept with the
        project.

    reading:
        What can't be read is left out, or shown as missing, rather than
        stopping the rest from being read.

shape RankedSelectionListShape:
    description:
        A list of ranked rows, beside it the details of the row selected, and
        along the bottom how many are checked and what to do with them. Each use
        names what it ranks and how, what its rows and details add, which rows
        start checked, and its action.

    rows:
        The rows are in the order ranked, the most worth first. Each row has a
        checkbox, the name of what it ranks, and a bar and percentage for how
        much it is worth, then whatever the use adds. A row that can't be
        chosen has its checkbox unchecked and disabled, and says why, muted.
        The list scrolls with a @{ScrollbarScope}. With nothing ranked, the use
        says why in place of the list.

    details:
        Clicking a row selects it, and beside the list, the selected row's
        details show. The row ranked first is selected to start with.

    action:
        Along the bottom, how many rows are checked, as "No …", "1 …", or
        "N …" followed by what the use ranks and "checked", and a primary
        button for the use's action, disabled with none checked.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope
from /ui/components/git-panel import GitPanelScope

export scope PromptModesScope:
    concept: {PromptModesConcept}

concept PromptModesConcept:
    pitch:
        The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the
        code and the spec.

    shape: {PromptModesShape}

shape PromptModesShape:
    description:
        There are four modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this
        order, each with what it is for and its colour:
        - Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
        - Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
        - Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
        - Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green

    colours:
        Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's
        colour, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec
        together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple.

    tasks:
        A prompt sent in Code, Chain, or Spec is a task, sent as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. Tasks carry on one conversation, one at a
        time, and queue while the harness is working. Before one is sent, the
        spec is built ahead of it, as the @{SpecBuildScope} says. Once one
        finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to
        the @{GitPanelScope}.

    questions:
        A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside
        any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or
        adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own,
        apart from the tasks', as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

    systemPrompts:
        Each mode sends its own system prompt, from the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope}. A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while
        it waits in the queue.

concept ProjectLocationsConcept:
    pitch:

shape ProjectLocationsShape:
    description:
        A project's locations are set in the piton.config.pi of the
        @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, each a path relative to the project directory:
        - the spec location is `root`, of its piton-config anchor
        - the code location is `codeRoot`, of its belay-config framework

        A location missing from the config is left out of whatever would use
        it, or, where it can't be left out, what needs it says it couldn't be
        read.

    listingFiles:

        directory, are every file at any depth, hidden ones included, leaving
        out `.git` and whatever the project's `.gitignore` files ignore. They
        are shown by their path relative to the project, and sorted by it.

        The spec files are the .pi files under the spec location, and the
        source files are the files under the code location. A use can leave
        out more, or cap how many it takes.
