use /lib
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope

export scope ModeSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {ModeSystemPromptsConcept}

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        Each of the @{PromptModesScope} has a system prompt template. A prompt
        sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property,
        alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

    templates:
        A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can
        reference the spec, with two placeholders, CODE_LOCATION and
        SPEC_LOCATION, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a
        Piton interpolation. Before the prompt is compiled, they are filled in
        with the code location and the spec location, as the
        @{ProjectLocationsScope} says.

    saving:
        Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}. A mode with no file yet sends its default.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown
        file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth
        for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built,
        so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing
        them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
        without them.

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        template puts back.

use /lib
from /scope/prompt-mode import PromptEditor
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope

export scope PromptSendingScope:
    concept: {PromptSendingConcept}

concept PromptSendingConcept:
    pitch:
        How a prompt gets to the harness, whether written in the chat input or
        sent on the application's behalf.

    shape: {PromptSendingShape}

shape PromptSendingShape:
    description:
        A prompt is sent in one of the @{PromptModesScope}, with anything
        attached to it. Sending is never blocked by the harness working.

    tasks:
        A task, a prompt in Code, Chain, or Spec, is sent straight away while
        the harness is free. While the harness is working, it waits in the
        @{PromptEditor}'s queue instead, in the order it was sent, keeping its
        mode and attachments, until its turn comes.

        When a task is actually sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the
        @{SpecBuildScope} says, the task showing "Building" until the build is
        over; then its hidden anchor is compiled and run. It heads the
        @{MessageList} as the latest task, and is saved in the prompt history,
        as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. A prompt that fails to compile or run
        fails its task, and doesn't stop the queue.

    questions:
        A question, a prompt in Ask, never queues: it runs straight away, even
        while the harness is working on a task or other questions, joins the
        questions stacked above the @{ChatInputScope}'s tabs, and is saved
        among the questions asked.

    onTheApplicationsBehalf:
        Something in the application can send a prompt as if it were written in
        the chat input and sent from one of its tabs. It goes just the same
        way: queued if the harness is busy, shown as a task, and entered in the
        history. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it,
        is left alone.

        opens nothing.

export scope HarnessCatalogScope:
    concept: {HarnessCatalogConcept}

    pitch:
        The skills, commands, and agents the harness has, so they can be found
        and used in a prompt the way they are in the harness itself.

    shape: {HarnessCatalogShape}

shape HarnessCatalogShape:
    description:
        What the @{HarnessIntegrationScope}'s harness has to offer, each one a
        skill, a command, or an agent, with its name, and its description when
        it has one.

    sources:
        Skills and commands are those of the @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, of the
        user, and of the user's enabled plugins, a plugin's own being named
        `plugin:name`. Agents come from the same places, plus the harness's
        built-in agents.

        Every harness run reports the skills and agents it has, built-in ones
        included. The last report is saved with the project's data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, and offered too.

    mentioning:
        A skill or command is used in a prompt as `/name `, and an agent as
        `@agent-name `, which the harness understands as a request to use that
        agent. They pass through the hidden anchor and its compilation
        unchanged, so a prompt starting with `/name` runs that skill or
        command.

use /lib

export scope UserPreferencesScope:
    concept: {UserPreferencesConcept}

concept UserPreferencesConcept:
    pitch:
        The choices the application remembers for the user, rather than for a
        project, so each launch starts as the last one left off.

    shape: {UserPreferencesShape}

shape UserPreferencesShape:
    description:
        Preferences are remembered for the user across launches and across all
        projects, in the platform's per-user config directory, never in a
        project. They are:
        - light or dark mode, which, until chosen, follows the operating system's appearance
        - whether the ribbon is collapsed, which starts expanded
        - the layout of a file's diff, which starts side by side
        - the recent projects
        - the folder a project was last opened from

        A preference is saved as soon as it is chosen, and restored on the next
        launch.

    failing:
        A preference that can't be saved still holds for the rest of the
        session. Only dark mode says so, as its command does; the others fail
        quietly, being only a convenience.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration/baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/harness-integration/one-off-run import OneOffAgentRunScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/running-activity import RunningActivityScope
from /ui/components/minimizable-panel import MinimizablePanelScope
from /ui/components/ranked-selection-list import RankedSelectionListScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export scope RescopeScope:
    concept: {RescopeConcept}

concept RescopeConcept:
    pitch:
        Finds concepts the spec describes over and over in different scopes
        that would be better as scopes of their own, ranks them, and hands the
        ones chosen to the harness to refactor the spec around them.

    shape: {RescopeShape}

shape RescopeShape:
    description:
        A @{MinimizablePanelScope} titled "Rescope". Opening it starts looking
        straight away. Once it is over, a "Look again" button in the header
        starts afresh.

    minimizing:
        Its minimize button's tooltip says the search keeps running. While it
        runs, it is listed among the @{RunningActivityScope} as
        "Finding scopes to extract". The Rescope command brings back a
        minimized panel as it was, without looking again.

    looking:
        steps:
            While it runs, the panel lists its steps, "Reading the spec" and
            "Looking for repeated concepts", each with a spinner while it runs,
            a tick once done, or a cross and why if it failed.

        agent:
            First the panel lists the spec files, as the
            @{ProjectLocationsScope} says. Then a @{OneOffAgentRunScope} looks
            through them. Its prompt is rescope.pi, of the
            @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, with the list of spec files after it.
            It replies, for each repeated concept worth a scope of its own, with
            a name for the scope, a sentence on what the concept is, from 0 to 1
            how much extracting it is worth, a sentence on why, and each place
            the spec describes it, with the file, the scope there, and a short

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration/baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/harness-integration/one-off-run import OneOffAgentRunScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /ui/components/inset-panel import InsetPanelScope
from /ui/components/minimizable-panel import MinimizablePanelScope
from /ui/components/ranked-selection-list import RankedSelectionListScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export scope GenerateSkillsScope:
    concept: {GenerateSkillsConcept}

concept GenerateSkillsConcept:
    pitch:
        Finds which of the spec's scopes are the most connected and the most
        used, ranks them for the skills that could and should be built for
        them, and adds the skills chosen to the spec, each building its scope.

    shape: {GenerateSkillsShape}

shape GenerateSkillsShape:
    description:
        An @{InsetPanelScope} titled "Generate Skills", with a close button.
        Opening it maps the spec and ranks its scopes straight away. Unlike a
        @{MinimizablePanelScope}, it can't be minimized: closing the panel
        while it runs stops it. Once it is over, a "Rank again" button in the
        header starts afresh.

    mapping:
        First, without the harness, the panel maps the spec: every spec file,
        as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says. A scope is each scope a file
        exports, the file it's in, and the path it's imported from, the file's
        path within the spec location without its .pi, and without a trailing
        /index. A scope references another each time a file of its own names
        the other with an at-brace or a dollar-brace reference; references to
        itself don't count. Each scope is used by the scopes that reference it,
        and uses those it references, each connection with how many times. A
        scope already has a skill when a skill in the spec's agent/skills
        folder builds it: its scope is that scope, or it is named Build, then
        the scope's name without a trailing Scope, and imports it. A skill that
        only mentions a scope doesn't count.

    ranking:
        steps:
            While it runs, the panel lists its steps, "Mapping the spec" and
            "Ranking scopes for skills", each with a spinner while it runs, a
            tick once done, or a cross and why if it failed.

        agent:
            Then a @{OneOffAgentRunScope} ranks the scopes. Its prompt is
            generate-skills.pi, of the @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, with the map
            of the spec after it: each scope, its file, how many scopes use it
            and how many it uses, and whether it already has a skill. It
            replies, for each scope worth a skill, with from 0 to 1 how much a
            skill for it is worth, whether one should be built rather than only
            could be, and a sentence on why.

        progress:
            Beneath the steps, the run's output shows in its
            @{TaskTableScope}.

        failing:
            When the run fails, the step says why, and the scopes are still
            offered, ranked by how connected they are alone, with a note saying
            the harness couldn't rank them.

    results:
        list:
            Once ranked, the panel lists the scopes in a
            @{RankedSelectionListScope}: those the harness named, most worth a
            skill first, then any others ranked by how connected they are,
            those used by the most scopes first, then those using the most.
            Each row has the scope's name, how much a skill is worth, how many
            scopes use it and how many it uses, and "Should" or "Could". The
            scopes it says should have a skill start checked. A scope that
            already has a skill can't be chosen, and reads "Has a skill".

        details:
            The selected scope's details are its name, its file, why the
            harness ranked it as it did, then "Used by" and "Uses", each listing
            the scopes on that side of its connections, most references first,
            each with a bar as long as its share of the most references there,
            and how many. Clicking one of those selects that scope.

        creating:
            The list's action is "Create Skills", counting scopes. It writes a
            skill into the spec for each scope checked: a file in the spec's
            agent/skills folder named Build, then the scope's name without a
            trailing Scope, then .pi, that imports the scope and exports a
            skill building it. When the spec has a build-scope keyword, from
            lib/agent/skills/BuildScope.pi, the skill is a build-scope with the
            scope as its scope; otherwise it is a skill of its own, whose
            description and useWhen say it builds or changes the scope, and
            whose prompt says to build it from the spec, the spec being the
            source of truth. The skills folder's index.pi exports each new
            skill, created if it isn't there, and when the agent folder is new,
            its index.pi exports the skills and the spec's index.pi exports the
            agent folder. A file already there is never overwritten, and its
            scope is left out.

            Once written, the rows for the new skills read "Has a skill", and a
            note says how many were created, and to build the spec for them to
            be written for the agents. A skill that couldn't be written says
            why in the note.

content.content:
Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown
        on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered
        into groups.

    sentPrompt:
        A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to
        the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the
        name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.

    status:
        A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in
        blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green,
        "Failed" in red, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history
        with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and
        dark mode.

    outputTable:
        A task's output is a @{TaskTableScope}, whose rows are what the harness
        did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the
        waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse
        their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.

    links:
        Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to
        a file opens it, as the @{OpenFileScope} says, and a web link opens in
        the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is
        shown as a link and opens that file the same way.

    backgrounds:
        The header for the latest task is coloured like the tab the task was
        sent from, the colour of its mode, of the @{PromptModesScope}, as the
        @{ChatInputScope} body shows for that tab. A task from the history that doesn't say which tab it was sent
        from keeps the tab bar's colour. The queue along the bottom and the
        previous tasks row along the top both have the same background colour as
        the tab bar.

    askDimming:
        While the @{AnswerDrawerScope} is open, it dims the message list beneath
        it.

    scrolling:
        The latest task's table scrolls with its lock to the bottom off to
        start with, until switched on.

        However long the list of previous tasks grows, drawing it costs no more
        than drawing the tasks in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output
        stay smooth.

            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

            It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the
            @{PromptModesScope} says.

    colour:
            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the
            colour of its mode, of the @{PromptModesScope}. With Chain selected,
            Code, Spec, and the body are all purple.
            The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes,
            straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap
            around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's
            red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green;
            neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.

    systemPrompt:
        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system
        prompt is sent with it, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

    ask:
        Ask is for simply asking a question. A question runs straight away,
        separately from any Code, Chain, or Spec task, even while the harness is
        working on one. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run
        at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already
        running.

        Each question's progress and results are shown in a
        @{TaskTableScope}. The questions stack directly above the tabs, the
        newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make
        room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is
        ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an
        animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While
        the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest
        thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and
        first line.

        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
        and first line, above its full task table, in the @{AnswerDrawerScope},
        which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to
        the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time: opening another
        closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the
        stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down
        to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it
        again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it
        if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question
        becomes a previous answer.

    answerSteps:
        For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished
        question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer,
        the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the
        @{TaskTableScope} says. A question closed into the previous answers
        starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the
        @{MessageList}.

    previousAnswers:
        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
        "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the
        @{AnswerDrawerScope}, sliding up from on top of any question rows still
        in the stack, as the drawer does for the previous answers. The
        questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them
        left off.

    answerDrawer: @{AnswerDrawerScope}

    selectingAnswerText:
        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.

        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
        popover also closes when the drawer closes.

    attachments:
        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.

        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
        the attachments it was sent with.

    escape:
        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
        input.

    growToFit:
        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at
        most. Its single row lines up with the send button.

    autoFocus:
        The chat input should be auto-focused.

    syntaxHighlighting:
        Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter
        Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

    lsp: @{LSP}

use /lib
from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
from /ui/components/selection-popover import SelectionPopoverScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/harness-integration/catalog import HarnessCatalogScope
from /scope/lsp import LSP
from /scope/prompt-mode/answer-drawer import AnswerDrawerScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /ui/components/history-list import HistoryListScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export scope ChatInputScope:
    concept: {ChatInputConcept}

concept ChatInputConcept:
    pitch:
        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
        as snippets of Piton.

    shape: {ChatInputShape}

shape ChatInputShape:
    description:
        Input on the left, send button on the right.

        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}

        Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. While the harness is working, the send
        button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue", since the
        prompt will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a
        question is never queued. The button is only disabled
        while the input is empty.

    tabs:
        overview:
            The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using
            gpui-kit's default tab styling. There is a tab for each of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask.
            Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain
            is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All
            four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has
            more padding than a normal tab.

            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.

            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
            Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
            not <Cmd>.

            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
            either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

        chain:
            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
            selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its
            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
            is selected.

            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
            them.

            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
            Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified
            tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent
            background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec
            show through underneath it.

        help:
            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

            It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the
            @{PromptModesScope} says.

        colour:
            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the
            colour of its mode, of the @{PromptModesScope}. With Chain selected,
            Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes,
            straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap
            around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's
            red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green;
            neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.

    systemPrompt:
        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system
        prompt is sent with it, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

    ask:
        Ask is for simply asking a question. A question runs straight away,
        separately from any Code, Chain, or Spec task, even while the harness is
        working on one. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run
        at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already
        running.

        Each question's progress and results are shown in a
        @{TaskTableScope}. The questions stack directly above the tabs, the
        newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make
        room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is
        ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an
        animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While
        the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest
        thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and
        first line.

        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
        and first line, above its full task table, in the @{AnswerDrawerScope},
        which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to
        the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time:
        opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the
        stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down
        to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it
        again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it
        if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question
        becomes a previous answer.

    answerSteps:
        For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished
        question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer,
        the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the
        @{TaskTableScope} says. A question closed into the previous answers
        starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the
        @{MessageList}.

    previousAnswers:
        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
        "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the
        @{AnswerDrawerScope}, sliding up from on top of any question rows still
        in the stack. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them
        left off.

    answerDrawer: @{AnswerDrawerScope}

    selectingAnswerText:
        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.

        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
        popover also closes when the drawer closes.

    attachments:
        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.

        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
        the attachments it was sent with.

    escape:
        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
        input.

    growToFit:
        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at
        most. Its single row lines up with the send button.

    autoFocus:
        The chat input should be auto-focused.

    syntaxHighlighting:
        Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter
        Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

    lsp: @{LSP}

    harnessMentions:
        overview:
            Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@`
            offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself.
            The placeholder mentions both.

        trigger:
            A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after
            whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at
            sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference.
            Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after
            each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that
            follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger;
            outside of one they never reach the @{LSP}.

        offered:
            The skills, commands, and agents offered are the
            @{HarnessCatalogScope}'s. Each shows whether it is a skill, command,
            or agent, and its description as documentation when it has one.
            Results are narrowed and ordered
            like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before
            matches anywhere in it, then by name.

        accepting:
            Accepting one inserts it as a mention, as the
            @{HarnessCatalogScope} says, in place of what was typed of it.
            Mentions work without the @{LSP}.

    hiddenAnchor:
        While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes,
        they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt
        property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope}

        escaping:
            A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it
            isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, quotes,
            colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and
            backslashes all mean something. Its userPrompt is a list with an
            item per line of the prompt, in order, and each line a list of its
            pieces: the text between references as a quoted string, with
            quotes, backslashes, and each dollar-brace escaped, so nothing in it
            is interpolated or evaluated; and each at-brace or dollar-brace
            around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported as
            a reference of its own. A reference to a name that isn't imported,
            such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. An empty line is a
            single empty string. The compiled userPrompt is the pieces of each
            line joined together, and the lines joined by line breaks, so what
            the harness receives is exactly what was typed or pasted, line for
            line, with each reference resolved. The systemPrompt is written the
            same way. A prompt saved as prose by an earlier version still reads
            back.

        autoImports:
            The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there,
            typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the
            prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position
            for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other
            than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out,
            character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or
            brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment
            then never stops the server finding the names that need importing,
            both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

        attachedText:
            A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText
            property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the
            order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not
            as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a
            quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it
            is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no
            attachedText property.

            What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the
            attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a
            fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks
            in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the
            task's header.

its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the
        hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the
        harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it
        has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead.

    queue:
        overview:
            The queue holds the tasks sent while the harness is working, as the
            @{PromptSendingScope} says, in the order they were sent, and sends
            them one at a time.

        placement:
            The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and
            directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is
            not part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued,
            with a chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line
            or two of each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list
            is numbered, with its number, text, and cancel button vertically
            centred in its row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a
            @{ScrollbarScope}. Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to
            the bottom, on the prompts queued most recently, however it was
            scrolled when last closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch
            and the "Send next" button.
            The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.

        cancel:
            A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which
            removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no
            longer in the queue.

        autoSend:
            A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending the next
            queued prompt as soon as the harness is free, and waiting. It starts
            switched on. Switching it on while the harness is free sends the
            next queued prompt straight away. Whenever the harness is free and
            the queue is not empty, a "Send next" button sends the first queued
            prompt.

        persistence:
            Queued prompts are saved with the project's data as they are
            queued, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The queue is restored whenever the project is opened;
            a restored queue waits for "Send next" rather than sending on its
            own. A queued prompt's file is removed when it is cancelled, or
            when it is sent, at which point it is saved to the prompt history
            like any other prompt.

    buildingTheSpec:
        A task builds the spec before it is sent, as the @{PromptModesScope}
        says, since the task may be the one to fix the spec, its output
        starting with an error saying the build failed when it does.

    history:
        Every task sent is saved in the prompt history with the project's data,
        as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, and its record once its run is over.
        Opening the project brings back every task in order, with its output replayed from
        that record. A task with no record shows as "Not recorded".

        Every question asked from the Ask tab is logged the same way, but among
        the questions instead, so it never comes back as a task. The record is saved when the run is over, and also
        when the question is closed or replaced while it runs, with as much as
        the harness had done. A question that fails before it reaches the
        harness is logged too, with the error in its record.

    chatInput: @{ChatInputScope}

grep -n "GitPanelScope\|MessageList\|HistoryListScope\|ScrollbarScope" spec/scope/prompt-mode/index.pi | head; cat > /tmp/reflow.py <<'EOF'
import sys,re,textwrap
KEY=re.compile(r'^\s*[A-Za-z][\w-]*:(\s|$)')
for p in sys.argv[1:]:
    lines=open(p).read().split('\n'); out=[]; i=0
    while i<len(lines):
        l=lines[i]
        ind=len(l)-len(l.lstrip())
        def prose(x):
            return x.strip() and not x.lstrip().startswith('- ') and not KEY.match(x) and not x.lstrip().startswith(('use ','from ','export ','concept ','shape ','scope '))
        if prose(l) and ind>=8:
            j=i
            while j<len(lines) and prose(lines[j]) and len(lines[j])-len(lines[j].lstrip())==ind: j+=1
            block=lines[i:j]
            if any(len(x)>80 for x in block):
                text=' '.join(x.strip() for x in block)
                out+=textwrap.wrap(text,width=80,initial_indent=' '*ind,subsequent_indent=' '*ind,break_long_words=False,break_on_hyphens=False)
            else: out+=block
            i=j
        else:
            out.append(l); i+=1
    open(p,'w').write('\n'.join(out))
EOF

# Rescope Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Finds concepts the spec describes over and over in different scopes that would be better as scopes of their own, ranks them, and hands the ones chosen to the harness to refactor the spec around them.

### Shape

#### Description

A [MinimizablePanelScope](../../ui/components/minimizable-panel/MinimizablePanelScope.md) titled "Rescope". Opening it starts looking straight away. Once it is over, a "Look again" button in the header starts afresh.

#### Minimizing

Its minimize button's tooltip says the search keeps running. While it runs, it is listed among the [RunningActivityScope](../running-activity/RunningActivityScope.md) as "Finding scopes to extract". The Rescope command brings back a minimized panel as it was, without looking again.

#### Looking

```
steps: While it runs, the panel lists its steps, "Reading the spec" and "Looking for repeated concepts", each with a spinner while it runs, a tick once done, or a cross and why if it failed.
agent: First the panel lists the spec files, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/ProjectLocationsScope.md) says. Then a [OneOffAgentRunScope](../harness-integration/one-off-run/OneOffAgentRunScope.md) looks through them. Its prompt is rescope.pi, of the [BakedSystemPromptsScope](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/BakedSystemPromptsScope.md), with the list of spec files after it. It replies, for each repeated concept worth a scope of its own, with a name for the scope, a sentence on what the concept is, from 0 to 1 how much extracting it is worth, a sentence on why, and each place the spec describes it, with the file, the scope there, and a short excerpt.
progress: Beneath the steps, the run's output shows in its [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/TaskTableScope.md).
failing: When the run fails, the step says why, and nothing is offered.
```

#### Results

```
list: Once found, the panel lists the concepts in a [RankedSelectionListScope](../../ui/components/ranked-selection-list/RankedSelectionListScope.md), most worth extracting first, those with the most places after, each row with the proposed scope's name, how much it is worth, and in how many places and how many scopes the spec describes it. Those worth half or more start checked. With none found, the panel says the spec repeats no concepts worth a scope of their own.
details: The selected concept's details are its proposed name, what it is, why it is worth extracting, then "Where the spec describes it", each place with its scope, its file, muted, and its excerpt in the editor's monospace font.
```

#### Refactoring

The list's action is "Refactor", counting concepts. Pressing it closes the panel and sends a prompt in Spec mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../prompt-mode/modes/PromptModesScope.md), on the application's behalf, as the [PromptSendingScope](../prompt-mode/sending/PromptSendingScope.md) says. The prompt is the refactoring request from rescope.pi, then each checked concept: its name, what it is, and every place the spec describes it, asking for each to become a scope of its own that those places reference instead of describing it again.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

All 17 concepts are now scopes of their own. Every listed place refers to its scope and keeps only what's particular to it. `piton check` (95 files), `piton build check` and `piton build` (wrote 79 files) all pass, and each new scope has its reference page for the agents. - **In `ui/components/`:**
  - `task-table`: TaskTableScope
  - `minimizable-panel`: MinimizablePanelScope
  - `ranked-selection-list`: RankedSelectionListScope
- **Harness (`scope/harness-integration/`):**
  - `one-off-run`: OneOffAgentRunScope
  - `baked-prompts`: BakedSystemPromptsScope
  - `catalog`: HarnessCatalogScope

- **Prompt mode (`scope/prompt-mode/`):**
  - `modes`: PromptModesScope
  - `sending`: PromptSendingScope
  - `answer-drawer`: AnswerDrawerScope
  - `mode-system-prompts`: ModeSystemPromptsScope
- **In `scope/`:**
  - `spec-build`: SpecBuildScope
  - `running-activity`: RunningActivityScope
